fuentes/texto-de-anitta/resumen.texto: Third-person account of the conquests of Pithana and of Anitta of Kussara, among them Neša, Hattusa and Zalpuwa, and of the curse pronounced against Hattusa. It is the oldest known text written in Hittite, and also in an Indo-European language.

fuentes/texto-de-anitta/por_que_importa.texto: It recounts the rivalry between the southern branch (Kussara, Neša) and the northern branch (Zalpuwa, Hattusa) of the royal family. Scholars debate whether it is Anitta's own work or a later compilation, and whether its original was in Akkadian.

fuentes/anales-de-hattusili-i/soporte.texto: Bilingual clay tablet (copy from the 13th century BC)

fuentes/anales-de-hattusili-i/resumen.texto: Bilingual tablet in Hittite and Akkadian recounting five years of campaigns by Hattusili I: Zalpa and Sanahuitta, Syrian cities allied with Yamhad, Arzawa, and the crossing of the Euphrates. It survives in a later copy; Bryce dates it to the 13th century BC.

fuentes/anales-de-hattusili-i/por_que_im.texto: It is the oldest direct source on the Hittite wars in Syria and on the beginning of the empire.

fuentes/testamento-de-hattusili-i/soport.texto: Clay tablet (copy from the 13th century BC)

fuentes/testamento-de-hattusili-i/resume.texto: First-person proclamation by Hattusili I, sick and wounded after his last campaign, who rejects his nephew as heir and names his grandson Mursili I. It is classified as CTH 6 and survives in a late copy.

fuentes/testamento-de-hattusili-i/por_qu.texto: It is one of the earliest Hittite texts on succession and shows the conflicts within the royal family.

fuentes/edicto-de-telipinu/resumen.texto: Edict of Telipinu (CTH 19), which reviews the crimes and murders at court since Hattusili I and establishes a rule of succession. It is the main source for reconstructing the sequence of kings of the Old Kingdom, and it records the conquest of Babylon by Mursili I, which is not attested in any other Hittite document.

fuentes/edicto-de-telipinu/por_que_impor.texto: According to Van Seters it is a legal text rather than a historical one; Lawson replies that a nearly legal text can also be historical.

fuentes/tratado-de-sunassura/resumen.texto: Treaty between Tudhaliya I/II and Sunassura of Kizzuwatna, which marks the end of Kizzuwatna's independence. Versions of earlier treaties between equals and of the agreement of subordination survive.

fuentes/tratado-de-sunassura/por_que_imp.texto: It shows how the Hittites absorbed Kizzuwatna, which controlled the passage between Anatolia and Syria. Some specialists believe there were two Sunassuras.

fuentes/acusacion-contra-madduwatta/resu.texto: Hittite text (CTH 147) written under Arnuwanda I, recalling the violations of his oaths by Madduwatta, a vassal installed in Zippasla by Tudhaliya I/II. It contains the first mention of Ahhiyawa, in the form Ahhiya, and the name Attarsiya.

fuentes/acusacion-contra-madduwatta/por_.texto: It is the oldest testimony to the presence of the Ahhiyawa, possibly Mycenaean, in western Anatolia. It is not known whether it was a legal document, a diplomatic warning or a draft.

fuentes/tratado-de-mursili-ii-con-manapa.texto: Treaty of Mursili II with Manapa-Tarhunta

Treaty (CTH 69) by which Mursili II confirms Manapa-Tarhunta as king of the Land of the Seha River after the Arzawan rebellion. It is one of the sources on the organization of the vassals of western Anatolia.
Together with the treaties with Mira and Hapalla, it shows the network of vassals in western Anatolia after the fall of Arzawa.

fuentes/tratado-de-mursili-ii-con-kupant.texto: Treaty of Mursili II with Kupanta-Kurunta of Mira

Treaty (CTH 68) by which Mursili II installs Kupanta-Kurunta as king of Mira and cedes him Kuwaliya, with the border at the Astarpa River. It is a source on the geography and politics of western Anatolia.
Its Astarpa border also appears in the annals of Mursili and in the debate over the Milawata letter.

fuentes/anales-de-mursili-ii/resumen.texto: Annals (CTH 61) of the first ten years of Mursili II, and an expanded version, recounting campaigns against the Kaska, against Uhha-Ziti of Arzawa and against Hayasa-Azzi, together with the eclipse of his tenth year. They are the main source for these events.

fuentes/anales-de-mursili-ii/por_que_imp.texto: The eclipse recorded in them is one of the anchor points of Hittite chronology; the most widely accepted date is 1312 BC.

fuentes/hechos-de-suppiluliuma/resumen.texto: Account composed by Mursili II of the campaigns and diplomacy of his father Suppiluliuma I: the war against Mitanni, the capture of Karkemish, and the episode of Zannanza and the widowed queen of Egypt.

fuentes/hechos-de-suppiluliuma/por_que_i.texto: It is the most complete source on Hittite expansion in Syria and the only one to recount the dispatch of a Hittite prince to Egypt.

fuentes/oraciones-de-la-plaga-de-mursili.texto: Prayers (CTH 378) in which Mursili II asks the gods to end the epidemic that ravaged the kingdom and looks for its causes in the sins of his father. They are linked to the Hittite plague.
They document an epidemic lasting decades in the Hittite kingdom, which scholarship debates as possibly tularemia.

fuentes/tratado-de-suppiluliuma-i-con-sh.texto: Treaty of Suppiluliuma I with Shattiwaza of Mitanni

Pair of texts (CTH 51 and 52) with the history of Mitanni from the Hittite point of view and the oath of vassalage of Shattiwaza, son of Tushratta, to Suppiluliuma I. It is almost the only source on the reign of Shattiwaza and the mention of Indo-Aryan gods.
It names Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya among the guarantor gods: it is the oldest written testimony to these gods.

fuentes/tratado-de-alaksandu/titulo.texto: Treaty of Muwatalli II with Alaksandu of Wilusa

fuentes/tratado-de-alaksandu/resumen.texto: Treaty between Muwatalli II and Alaksandu, king of Wilusa, which recalls more than three centuries of friendship between Hatti and Wilusa. It requires the king to have the text read publicly three times a year.

fuentes/tratado-de-alaksandu/por_que_imp.texto: By counting Wilusa among the lands of Arzawa, north of the Land of the Seha River, it supports its identification with Troy, which is still debated.

fuentes/carta-de-tawagalawa/resumen.texto: Letter (CTH 181) from a Hittite king, generally identified with Hattusili III, to the king of Ahhiyawa, whom he calls brother, asking for help in subduing Piyamaradu. It recalls an earlier hostility over Wilusa that was settled by peace.

fuentes/carta-de-tawagalawa/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the few windows on relations between the Hittites and the Mycenaean Greeks. Scholars debate who wrote it: Hattusili III or Muwatalli II.

fuentes/carta-de-milawata/resumen.texto: Letter (CTH 182) from a Hittite king to a vassal king of western Anatolia, demanding hostages and fugitives and asking him to hand over the claimant to Wilusa so that he can be restored to the throne. It mentions Milawata, Atriya and Piyamaradu as a figure of the past.

fuentes/carta-de-milawata/por_que_import.texto: It is central to the debate on the historicity of the Iliad. Its author is disputed (Tudhaliya IV according to Burney and Bryce), and so is its addressee (Kupanta-Kurunta or Tarkasnawa).

fuentes/apologia-de-hattusili-iii/resume.texto: Autobiographical account (CTH 81) in which Hattusili III justifies his accession to the throne against his nephew Mursili III. It tells of his sickly childhood, the protection of the goddess Ishtar, and his role as governor of the north.

fuentes/apologia-de-hattusili-iii/por_qu.texto: It is the main source for his youth, his reign and the civil war with Urhi-Teshub, although it is a text of justification.

fuentes/tablilla-de-bronce-de-hattusa/re.texto: The only Hittite metal tablet found so far, bearing the vassal treaty of Tudhaliya IV and his cousin Kurunta, king of Tarhuntassa. It describes in detail the borders of that kingdom and names Halwaziti as scribe.

fuentes/tablilla-de-bronce-de-hattusa/po.texto: It is a first-rate source on the geography of Bronze Age Anatolia and on politics within the royal family.

fuentes/inscripciones-de-suppiluliuma-ii.texto: Stone inscriptions (Nişantepe and chamber 2 of the east pool)

Two Luwian inscriptions from Hattusa recording campaigns of Suppiluliuma II in southwestern Anatolia (Wiyanawanda, Tamina, Masa, Lukka, Ikuna), against Tarhuntassa, and at sea off Alashiya. Chamber 2 was linked to the symbolic entrance to the underworld.
They are the last known imperial Hittite inscriptions and one of the few sources on the final years of the empire.

fuentes/relieve-de-karabel/resumen.texto: Rock relief in the Karabel pass, near İzmir, showing King Tarkasnawa of Mira and a Luwian hieroglyphic inscription naming him as son and grandson of kings of Mira. John David Hawkins read the text in 1998.

fuentes/relieve-de-karabel/por_que_impor.texto: It proved that Mira lay south of the Land of the Seha River, and that Wilusa must lie north of the Gediz River, in the Troad.

fuentes/cancion-de-ullikummi/resumen.texto: Hurrian mythic poem preserved in Hittite about the stone monster Ullikummi, son of Kumarbi and of a rock. It was found at Boğazköy with fragments in Hurrian.

fuentes/cancion-de-ullikummi/por_que_imp.texto: It is considered a precedent for Greek myths in Hesiod, such as Typhon; Güterbock (1951) edited it and Burkert pointed out the parallels.

fuentes/mito-de-illuyanka/resumen.texto: Hittite myth (CTH 321) in two consecutive versions about the storm god Tarhunz and the serpent Illuyanka. It was recited at the Hattian spring festival, the Puruli.

fuentes/mito-de-illuyanka/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the myths of the storm god's combat against a dragon, with parallels in other Near Eastern traditions.

fuentes/texto-de-kikkuli/resumen.texto: Treatise (CTH 284) in four tablets and about 1080 lines on training chariot horses, by Kikkuli, horse trainer of the land of Mitanni. It includes Indo-Aryan terms such as the numerals aika, tera, panza, satta and nawa.

fuentes/texto-de-kikkuli/por_que_importa.texto: It illustrates chariot technique and is evidence for the Indo-Aryan terms of Mitanni. The best surviving copy is Late Hittite, from the 13th century BC.

fuentes/cartas-de-tushratta/resumen.texto: Letters from Tushratta of Mitanni to Amenhotep III and Amenhotep IV, found at Amarna: offers of daughters in marriage, the sending of the statue of Shaushka of Nineveh, and complaints about gifts of gold. They include a long letter in the Hurrian language.

fuentes/cartas-de-tushratta/por_que_impo.texto: They are the main direct source on Mitanni and its diplomacy, since no native chronicle has been found.

fuentes/cartas-de-amarna-ea-31-y-32/titu.texto: Amarna Letters EA 31 and 32 with Arzawa

fuentes/cartas-de-amarna-ea-31-y-32/resu.texto: Pair of letters between Amenhotep III and Tarhuntaradu of Arzawa, in which the pharaoh proposes a diplomatic marriage and says he heard that Hattusa was paralyzed. Since Arzawa had no scribes for Akkadian, they were written in Hittite.

fuentes/cartas-de-amarna-ea-31-y-32/por_.texto: They show that Egypt recognized Arzawa as a great king at the moment of greatest Hittite weakness.

fuentes/archivos-de-hattusa/idioma_origi.texto: Hittite, Akkadian, Hurrian, Luwian and Hattic

fuentes/archivos-de-hattusa/resumen.texto: More than 30,000 cuneiform tablets and fragments from the royal archives of Hattusa, catalogued in the Catalogue of Hittite Texts (CTH): annals, treaties, letters, rituals, myths and laws. Copies were also found at Maşat, Ortaköy, Kuşaklı, Alalakh, Ugarit and Emar.

fuentes/archivos-de-hattusa/por_que_impo.texto: The corpus made it possible to decipher Hittite and to reconstruct the history of the kingdom and its neighbors.

fuentes/tablillas-de-tapikka/resumen.texto: 117 cuneiform tablets, mostly letters between the site and a king Tudhaliya, probably Tudhaliya III (Tudhaliya II in another numbering), found between 1973 and 1981 and edited by Sedat Alp in 1991. Most of them concern the front against the Kaska.

fuentes/tablillas-de-tapikka/por_que_imp.texto: It is the source on Hittite frontier administration; the exact span of time they cover is debated.

fuentes/archivos-de-sapinuwa/resumen.texto: About 5000 tablets and fragments from Building A at Sapinuwa, mostly in Hittite (some 1500) and Hurrian (some 600), with letters, rituals and bilingual vocabularies. They date to the end of the Middle Kingdom, the time of Tudhaliya III.

fuentes/archivos-de-sapinuwa/por_que_imp.texto: The archive yields bilingual Hittite-Hattic and Hittite-Hurrian texts that were not known before, although much of it is still unpublished.

fuentes/archivos-de-sarissa/resumen.texto: About 45 tablet fragments from Building A on the acropolis of Sarissa, containing ritual texts. They belong to the imperial stratum, destroyed by a fire in the second half of the 13th century BC.

fuentes/archivos-de-sarissa/por_que_impo.texto: They show the local cult and the life of a provincial center of the empire.

fuentes/carta-de-manapa-tarhunta/resumen.texto: Letter (CTH 191) from Manapa-Tarhunta, king of the Land of the Seha River, to the Hittite king. It names Piyamaradu, who had put Atpa in charge of the Land of the Seha River.

fuentes/carta-de-manapa-tarhunta/por_que.texto: It is one of three letters that, together with those of Tawagalawa and Milawata, speak of Piyamaradu and Ahhiyawa.

fuentes/carta-de-mitani/resumen.texto: Long letter from Tushratta, written in Hurrian and found at Amarna in 1887, with 494 lines of which 466 survive. It deals with the marriage of his daughter Tadukhepa to Amenhotep III.

fuentes/carta-de-mitani/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the main sources for the study of the Hurrian language.

fuentes/bryce-kingdom-of-the-hittites/re.texto: Trevor Bryce's synthesis of the political history and geography of the Hittite kingdom, from the Old Kingdom to the fall of the empire. The 2005 edition is a new, expanded version of the Oxford University Press edition of 1998. Its chronology, with the eclipse of Mursili II dated to 1312 BC, is the basis for the reign dates of this topic, especially in the 13th century BC.

fuentes/bryce-kingdom-of-the-hittites/po.texto: It is the most widely used academic reference for the series of Hittite kings, their vassals and their conflicts.

fuentes/beckman-hittite-diplomatic-texts.texto: Annotated translations of Hittite treaties and diplomatic letters with vassals, rivals and allies, by Gary Beckman, published in the series Writings from the Ancient World (volume 7) in 1996 and in a second edition in 1999. It gathers, among others, the treaties with Kizzuwatna, Mira, Seha, Wilusa, Amurru and Tarhuntassa.
It is the standard English edition of the texts on this topic that are treaties.

fuentes/hoffner-hittite-myths/resumen.texto: Translations of Hittite myths by Harry A. Hoffner Jr., including those of the vanishing god Telipinu, Illuyanka, Kumarbi and Ullikummi. Published in the series Writings from the Ancient World (volume 2) in 1990, and in an expanded second edition in 1998.

fuentes/hoffner-hittite-myths/por_que_im.texto: It gives access to the Hittite, Hurrian and Hattic mythic texts copied at Hattusa.

fuentes/chicago-hittite-dictionary/resum.texto: Dictionary of Hittite published by the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago (now ISAC), with citations from the texts of Hattusa. It is a reference for the language and institutions of the kingdom.

fuentes/chicago-hittite-dictionary/por_q.texto: It makes it possible to check the meaning of the Hittite words quoted in this topic.

fuentes/sagona-archaeology-of-the-caucas.texto: Antonio Sagona's synthesis of the archaeology of the Caucasus, from the first settlements to the Iron Age. It covers, among other topics, the Kura-Araxes, Maykop, Trialeti and Lchashen-Metsamor cultures.
It is a reference for dating and comparing the cultures of the Caucasus.

fuentes/kohl-making-of-bronze-age-eurasi.texto: The Making of Bronze Age Eurasia
Study by Philip L. Kohl of the Bronze Age societies of Eurasia, from the Balkans to Central Asia, with the Caucasus as a zone of contact. It is cited for the Maykop mound.
It places Maykop and Kura-Araxes within the metal exchange networks of Eurasia.

fuentes/blegen-troy/titulo.texto: Troy: Excavations Conducted by the University of Cincinnati, 1932-1938

fuentes/blegen-troy/resumen.texto: Excavation report by Carl Blegen and his team, published by Princeton University Press in four volumes (1950-1958), which divided the site into nine levels and 46 sublevels. It is the basis of the Troy I to IX sequence.

fuentes/blegen-troy/por_que_importa.texto: His stratigraphy remains the reference for the dates of Troy VI and VIIa.

fuentes/mito-de-telipinu/titulo.texto: Myth of Telipinu, the Vanishing God

fuentes/mito-de-telipinu/resumen.texto: Hittite myth of Hattian origin about the disappearance of the agrarian god Telipinu and its consequences for the land, until they bring him back. Versions survive on tablets from Hattusa.

fuentes/mito-de-telipinu/por_que_importa.texto: It is the best-known example of the vanishing-god type of myth, with parallels in other traditions.

fuentes/canciones-de-kumarbi/resumen.texto: Cycle of Hurrian myths about the god Kumarbi, preserved in Hittite, with Hurrian fragments found at Boğazköy. It includes the Song of Ullikummi and other tales of divine succession.

fuentes/canciones-de-kumarbi/por_que_imp.texto: It is compared with Hesiod's Theogony for its motif of succession among the gods.

fuentes/tablillas-de-tall-bazi/resumen.texto: Two cuneiform land-donation tablets from the Mitanni period, found in the temple of the citadel of Tall Bazi. A tablet of Artatama I granting land was also found at the site.

fuentes/tablillas-de-tall-bazi/por_que_i.texto: They are direct documents of Mitanni administration, of which almost no archives of its own survive.

fuentes/sello-de-shuttarna-de-alalakh/ti.texto: Seal of Shuttarna, son of Kirta

fuentes/sello-de-shuttarna-de-alalakh/re.texto: Seal found at Alalakh reading «Shuttarna, son of Kirta, king of Maitani». It is the only known contemporary evidence for Kirta and Shuttarna I.

fuentes/sello-de-shuttarna-de-alalakh/po.texto: It is the only epigraphic support for the tradition that Kirta founded the Mitanni dynasty, and the inscription is not very explicit.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-la-espada-de-assu.texto: Inscription on the Sword of Assuwa
Sword of possibly Mycenaean style found at Hattusa. Its inscription suggests that it was taken from a soldier of Assuwa and left as an offering to the Hittite storm god.
Eric Cline cites it among the signs that the Ahhiyawa may have supported Assuwa's rebellion against Tudhaliya I/II.

fuentes/tratado-de-suppiluliuma-i-con-hu.texto: Treaty of Suppiluliuma I with Hukkana of Hayasa

Vassal treaty between Suppiluliuma I and Hukkana (Hakkani), king of Hayasa, who had married a Hittite princess and then the sister of Suppiluliuma. It addresses “the people of Hayasa”, which Igor Diakonoff interpreted as evidence of an assembly or council of elders, and names Unag-astuas among its gods.
It is one of the few written sources on the political organization of Hayasa-Azzi.

fuentes/tablilla-de-tutulla/resumen.texto: Akkadian tablet found at İnandıktepe recording a land grant to the official Tutulla, bearing the tabarna seal, an archaic royal seal that names no particular king. These seals were used until the reigns of Telipinu and Alluwamna, so the tablet is dated to the late 16th century BC.

fuentes/tablilla-de-tutulla/por_que_impo.texto: Its seal dates the level of İnandıktepe where it was found.

fuentes/sello-luvita-de-troya/titulo.texto: Luwian Hieroglyphic Seal from Troy VIIb1

fuentes/sello-luvita-de-troya/resumen.texto: Bronze seal with Luwian hieroglyphs found in Troy VIIb1, with the name of a woman on one side and that of a man who worked as a scribe on the other. It is the only example of pre-Classical writing found at the site.

fuentes/sello-luvita-de-troya/por_que_im.texto: It is a possible sign of a Luwian-speaking population at Troy; its find context is debated, because the palace bureaucracies had already disappeared.

personas/pithana/resumen.texto: King of Kussara who, according to the Anitta text, took Neša (Kanesh) “at night, by force” without harming its inhabitants. His son Anitta succeeded him; the dates are approximate and the identification of Kussara is unresolved.

personas/anitta/resumen.texto: Son of Pithana, king of Kussara, who made Neša (Kanesh) his capital and, according to the text bearing his name, defeated Piyusti of Hatti and Huzziya of Zalpuwa. The Anitta text is the oldest known writing in Hittite; the dates of his reign (c. 1745-1720 BC according to one reconstruction) are approximate.

personas/piyusti/resumen.texto: King of Hattusa (Hatti) known only from the Anitta text, which mentions him as defeated by Anitta on at least two occasions. No inscriptions of his own survive; the date is approximate (around 1725 BC in this ordering, which makes him a contemporary of Anitta; other sources say around 1700 BC).

personas/labarna-i/roles.1.texto: traditionally the founder of the Old Kingdom

personas/labarna-i/resumen.texto: Regarded by Hittite tradition as the first king and founder of the Old Kingdom, at the beginning of the 17th century BC in Bryce's chronology. Some specialists doubt his existence, because “Labarna” was also a royal title, and the first to bear it may have been Hattusili I.

personas/hattusili-i/resumen.texto: King of the Hittite Old Kingdom who reigned c. 1650-1620 BC (Bryce's chronology), moved the capital from Neša to Hattusa and waged war in Syria. His annals, preserved in a later copy in Hittite and Akkadian, describe campaigns against Zalpa, Alalakh and Arzawa.

personas/hantili-i/resumen.texto: Cupbearer of Mursili I and married to his sister Harapsili, he murdered him with the help of his son-in-law Zidanta and succeeded him. He reigned c. 1590-1560 BC (Bryce's chronology); the Edict of Telipinu tells that he regretted the crime afterwards.

personas/zidanta-i/resumen.texto: Son-in-law of Hantili I, he helped him kill Mursili I and, according to the Edict of Telipinu, reached the throne after murdering the legitimate heir Piseni. He reigned c. 1560-1550 BC (Bryce's chronology), and his own son Ammuna killed him.

personas/ammuna/resumen.texto: Son of Zidanta I, whom he killed in order to reign c. 1550-1530 BC (Bryce's chronology). His reign was one of territorial losses: Hittite tradition records the rebellion of Kizzuwatna and of Arzawa, and a chronicle fragment shows him at war with Neša and other cities.

personas/huzziya-i/resumen.texto: Son of Ammuna who reigned about five years, c. 1530-1525 BC (Bryce's chronology). Telipinu, married to his sister, displaced him and exiled him; according to the Edict of Telipinu, Huzziya died later in exile.

personas/telipinu/roles.1.texto: last king of the Old Kingdom

personas/telipinu/resumen.texto: He reigned c. 1525-1500 BC (Bryce's chronology) and is the last king of the Old Kingdom. He promulgated the edict bearing his name, with the account of the earlier kings and a rule of succession, and made a treaty with Isputahsu of Kizzuwatna.

personas/tahurwaili/roles.0.texto: Hittite king of the Middle Kingdom

personas/tahurwaili/resumen.texto: Cousin of Telipinu and king of the Middle Kingdom, known from seal impressions found at Hattusa and from a letter of Telipinu. His place in the sequence of kings is uncertain; the middle chronology places him at the beginning of the 15th century BC. The order of the Middle Kingdom kings is uncertain: the dates are an approximate sequence, of low confidence.

personas/alluwamna/roles.0.texto: Hittite king of the Middle Kingdom

personas/alluwamna/resumen.texto: Son-in-law of Telipinu through his marriage to Harapseki, attested as great king by a seal. His exact place in the sequence of kings is disputed, and he is dated, without precision, to the 15th century BC. The order of the Middle Kingdom kings is uncertain: the dates are an approximate sequence, of low confidence.

personas/hantili-ii/roles.0.texto: Hittite king of the Middle Kingdom

personas/hantili-ii/resumen.texto: Son of Alluwamna, whom a land-grant document presents as his son. An endowment inscription found at Hattusa is attributed to him; his reign is placed without precision in the 15th century BC. The order of the Middle Kingdom kings is uncertain: the dates are an approximate sequence, of low confidence.

personas/zidanta-ii/roles.0.texto: Hittite king of the Middle Kingdom

personas/zidanta-ii/resumen.texto: Hittite king of the Middle Kingdom, in the 15th century BC, probably nephew of Hantili II. He made a treaty between equals with Pilliya of Kizzuwatna, the last that a Hittite king signed with a king of that country. The order of the Middle Kingdom kings is uncertain: the dates are an approximate sequence, of low confidence.

personas/huzziya-ii/roles.0.texto: Hittite king of the Middle Kingdom

personas/huzziya-ii/resumen.texto: Hittite king of the Middle Kingdom who, according to tradition, was murdered by Muwatalli I, chief of his royal guard. His reign falls without precision in the 15th century BC. The order of the Middle Kingdom kings is uncertain: the dates are an approximate sequence, of low confidence.

personas/muwatalli-i/roles.0.texto: Hittite king of the Middle Kingdom

personas/muwatalli-i/resumen.texto: Chief of the royal guard who killed Huzziya II and seized the throne; he was later murdered by Himuili and Kantuzzili. His reign falls without precision in the 15th century BC, shortly before Tudhaliya I. The order of the Middle Kingdom kings is uncertain: the dates are an approximate sequence, of low confidence.

personas/tudhaliya-i/resumen.texto: King whom some specialists consider identical with Tudhaliya II (Tudhaliya I/II), who reigned c. 1465-1440 BC (Bryce's chronology). The imperial period of the Hittites is usually said to begin with him; the numbering of the Tudhaliyas is debated.

personas/hattusili-ii/resumen.texto: Possible Hittite great king, c. 1440-1425 BC in Bryce's chronology. His existence as king is not certain: the data on him are scarce, and his place among the Tudhaliyas depends on the reconstruction followed.

personas/tudhaliya-ii/resumen.texto: Hittite king who reigned c. 1425-1390 BC (Bryce's chronology) and was father-in-law and predecessor of Arnuwanda I. Some specialists identify him with Tudhaliya I; the accusation against Madduwatta recounts events of his reign.

personas/arnuwanda-i/resumen.texto: Son-in-law and co-ruler of Tudhaliya II, he reigned c. 1390-1380 BC (Bryce's chronology). In his time the Kaska plundered Hittite holy cities, and the accusation against Madduwatta was written.

personas/tudhaliya-iii/resumen.texto: Son of Arnuwanda I, he reigned c. 1380-1350 BC (Bryce's chronology) and also bore the Hurrian name Tasmi-Sarri. Texts of his grandson Mursili II show the kingdom on the brink of collapse under attacks from all sides; according to one reconstruction he was the father-in-law and adoptive father of Suppiluliuma I, and according to another, his father.

personas/tudhaliya-el-joven/resumen.texto: Son and designated heir of Tudhaliya III, whom Suppiluliuma I had killed around 1350 BC. It is doubtful that he ever reigned; his murder was later considered the cause of a plague.

personas/arnuwanda-ii/resumen.texto: Eldest son of Suppiluliuma I and Henti, he reigned briefly c. 1322-1321 BC. Like his father, he died during the plague that ravaged the Hittites.

personas/mursili-ii/resumen.texto: Son of Suppiluliuma I who reigned c. 1321-1295 BC (Bryce's chronology, the same that places Muwatalli II c. 1295-1272; other reconstructions have him ascend the throne around 1330 BC). His annals recount the campaigns against the Kaska, Arzawa and Hayasa-Azzi, and he left prayers for the plague that struck the kingdom.

personas/tudhaliya-iv/resumen.texto: Son of Hattusili III and Puduhepa, he reigned c. 1237-1209 BC (Bryce's chronology; other reconstructions place him around 1245-1215 BC). He was defeated by Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria at Nihriya, built dams against a drought, and concluded the treaty of the bronze tablet with Kurunta of Tarhuntassa.

personas/kurunta/activo.lugar.texto: Tarhuntassa (unidentified site; approximate location per Wikidata)

personas/kurunta/resumen.texto: Youngest son of Muwatalli II and brother of Mursili III, whom his uncle Hattusili III made king of Tarhuntassa. Tudhaliya IV renewed his position in a treaty engraved on bronze; it has been proposed that he claimed the title of great king.

personas/arnuwanda-iii/resumen.texto: Penultimate king of the Hittite empire, who reigned briefly c. 1209-1207 BC (Bryce's chronology). Son of Tudhaliya IV, he was succeeded by his brother Suppiluliuma II.

personas/suppiluliuma-ii/resumen.texto: Last certain great Hittite king, son of Tudhaliya IV, who reigned c. 1207-1178 BC (Bryce's chronology). Two Luwian inscriptions of his recount campaigns in southwestern Anatolia and against Tarhuntassa and Alashiya; the capital was abandoned during or shortly after his reign.

personas/zannanza/resumen.texto: Son of Suppiluliuma I, sent to Egypt to marry the widow of a pharaoh, who died on the way. The episode, known from the Deeds of Suppiluliuma, damaged relations between Hittites and Egyptians.

personas/zita/resumen.texto: Brother of Suppiluliuma I and chief of the royal guard, who accompanied Arnuwanda II on the campaign against Mitanni in the Six Years' War. The dates are approximate.

personas/harapsili/resumen.texto: Queen of the Hittite Old Kingdom, sister of Mursili I and wife of Hantili I. She is named in the Edict of Telipinu among the relatives who suffered the court murders.

personas/henti/resumen.texto: First wife of Suppiluliuma I, daughter of Tudhaliya III (father or father-in-law and adoptive father of Suppiluliuma I, according to the reconstruction), who was Tawananna and mother of his legitimate children. Her seal calls her great queen; a damaged text suggests she was exiled toward Ahhiyawa.

personas/gassulawiya/resumen.texto: Hittite queen, first wife of Mursili II and mother of Muwatalli II and Hattusili III. Mursili dedicated a prayer to her for her illness, and, according to texts of his reign, her death was attributed to the Babylonian Tawananna.

personas/tanuhepa/resumen.texto: Second wife of Mursili II, with whom he had children whose names are not preserved. The dates are approximate and are placed around 1300 BC.

personas/piyassili/resumen.texto: Son of Suppiluliuma I, also called Sarri-Kusuh, who governed Karkemish after its capture. He led the Hittite army that installed Shattiwaza on the throne of Mitanni.

personas/talmi-teshub/roles.0.texto: king of Karkemish and Hittite viceroy

personas/talmi-teshub/resumen.texto: King of Karkemish and viceroy of the Hittite great king during the reign of Suppiluliuma II. He was in charge of affairs in Syria and oversaw the divorce of a daughter of the great king from the king of Ugarit.

personas/madduwatta/resumen.texto: Warlord of southwestern Anatolia, installed as king of Zippasla by Tudhaliya I/II, who repeatedly broke his oaths. He is known only from the Hittite accusation bearing his name, written under Arnuwanda I.

personas/attarsiya/resumen.texto: Warlord of Ahhiyawa mentioned in the accusation against Madduwatta, whom he attacked twice, and who raided Alashiya. He is the first attested Ahhiyawan personal name, and he is linked, without certainty, with Mycenaean Greece.

personas/piyamaradu/resumen.texto: Rebel chief of western Anatolia who, for about 35 years, challenged Muwatalli II, Hattusili III and Tudhaliya IV with the support of Ahhiyawa. He appears in the Tawagalawa letter; his sphere of action may have included Wilusa.

personas/alaksandu/resumen.texto: King of Wilusa, whom most identify with Troy (Hisarlık), who signed a treaty with Muwatalli II around 1280 BC. His name resembles the Greek Alexandros, and he has been associated with Paris of the Iliad, though this is unproven, and Alaksandu lived at least half a century before the period associated with the Trojan War.

personas/walmu/resumen.texto: King of Wilusa, whom most identify with Troy (Hisarlık), known only from the Milawata letter, which says that he was deposed and that the Hittites planned to restore him. The letter does not say who deposed him.

personas/manapa-tarhunta/roles.0.texto: king of the Land of the Seha River

personas/manapa-tarhunta/resumen.texto: King of the Land of the Seha River in western Anatolia, deposed by his brothers and restored to the throne with Hittite support. He allied with Uhha-Ziti of Arzawa, but Mursili II pardoned him and made a treaty with him.

personas/uhha-ziti/resumen.texto: Last independent king of Arzawa, who defied Mursili II and was defeated around 1320 BC according to the annals of Mursili. He fled to islands controlled by Ahhiyawa and died in exile.

personas/tarhuntaradu/resumen.texto: King of Arzawa in the first half of the 14th century BC, to whom Amenhotep III of Egypt wrote, addressing him as great king, in the Amarna letters EA 31 and 32. For lack of Akkadian scribes, the correspondence was written in Hittite.

personas/kupanta-kurunta/resumen.texto: King of Mira installed by Mursili II, who was his vassal and a relative through the marriage of Mashuiluwa to a daughter of Suppiluliuma I. He is a possible addressee of the Milawata letter and supported Hattusili III against Mursili III.

personas/tarkasnawa/resumen.texto: King of Mira, probably son of Alantalli and a contemporary of Tudhaliya IV, whose name appears on the Karabel relief in Luwian hieroglyphs and on a bilingual seal. He is proposed as the addressee of the Milawata letter.

personas/sunassura/resumen.texto: King of Kizzuwatna in the 15th century BC, who signed with Tudhaliya I/II a treaty that ended its independence. Some specialists believe there was a second Sunassura, the last independent king.

personas/pilliya/resumen.texto: King of Kizzuwatna in the 15th century BC, an ally of Mitanni, who made agreements with Idrimi of Alalakh and also with Zidanta II. The dates are approximate.

personas/isputahsu/resumen.texto: First known king of Kizzuwatna, whose seal was found at Tarsus bearing the name of his father Pariyawatri. He signed a treaty with Telipinu of Hatti.

personas/kikkuli/resumen.texto: Master horse trainer of the land of Mitanni and author of a text on preparing chariot horses, written mostly in Hittite. It contains Indo-Aryan terms and is relevant to the history of languages.

personas/kirta/roles.1.texto: traditionally the founder of the dynasty

personas/kirta/resumen.texto: Semi-legendary Hurrian king who, according to tradition, founded the Mitanni dynasty around 1540 BC. Epigraphic support is scarce: a seal from Alalakh names Shuttarna as son of Kirta, king of Maitani.

personas/shuttarna-i/resumen.texto: Early king of Mitanni, son of Kirta, known only from a seal found at Alalakh. He is said to have reigned around 1525 BC (middle chronology).

personas/parshatatar/resumen.texto: First king of Mitanni about whom there is clear information, who reigned c. 1510-1490 BC according to one reconstruction. Idrimi of Alalakh mentions him in his inscription as his sovereign; the name is written in several ways.

personas/shaushtatar/resumen.texto: King of Mitanni in the 15th century BC, who extended his rule as far as Assyria and Nuzi to the east and Kizzuwatna to the west. A later Hittite text says that he carried off the silver and gold doors of the palace of Assur.

personas/artatama-i/resumen.texto: King of Mitanni at the end of the 15th century BC, contemporary of Amenhotep II and Thutmose IV. According to the Amarna letters, his daughter married Thutmose IV.

personas/shuttarna-ii/resumen.texto: King of Mitanni at the beginning of the 14th century BC, who gave his daughter Gilukhepa in marriage to Amenhotep III. He was the father of Artashumara and Tushratta.

personas/artatama-ii/roles.0.texto: claimant to the throne of Mitanni

personas/artatama-ii/resumen.texto: Brother and rival of Tushratta for the throne, with whom Suppiluliuma I made a pact to weaken him. His son Shuttarna III later appears as a rival king.

personas/artashumara/resumen.texto: Son of Shuttarna II, who succeeded his father and was murdered by a pro-Hittite group led by Tuhi. He was replaced by his brother Tushratta.

personas/shuttarna-iii/resumen.texto: Usurper of the throne of Mitanni, who called himself king of the Hurrians and sought support from Assyria. He reigned briefly, at the end of the 14th century BC.

personas/shattiwaza/resumen.texto: Son of Tushratta who reigned c. 1327-1305 BC, a vassal of Suppiluliuma I, from whom he received a daughter in marriage. The two texts of the treaty they signed are almost the only source on his reign.

personas/wasashatta/resumen.texto: King of Mitanni at the beginning of the 13th century BC, successor of Shattuara I according to the reconstructed sequence of kings. He rebelled against Assyria and was defeated by Adad-nirari I; the sources that mention him are scarce.

personas/uhna/resumen.texto: King of Zalpuwa who, according to the Anitta text, sacked Kanesh and carried off the idol of the god Siu. His raid is dated around 1833 BC, and some link it with the fire of the karum.

personas/piyama-kurunta/resumen.texto: Son of King Uhha-Ziti of Arzawa, who according to the annals of Mursili II attacked Mira and lost to the Hittite army at Walma, by the Astarpa River. He surrendered, and Mursili deported him to Hattusa, where he probably died.

personas/kukkunni/resumen.texto: King of Wilusa (Wiluša, probably Hisarlık) at the end of the 14th century BC, mentioned in the treaty of Alaksandu as an ally of Suppiluliuma I. His reign coincides with the period of peace and prosperity of Troy VI; it is not known whether Alaksandu succeeded him immediately.

personas/daduhepa/resumen.texto: Hittite queen (tawananna) with a Hurrian name, wife of a Tudhaliya (also called Tasmi-Sarri), who is considered the father of Suppiluliuma I or, according to another reconstruction, his father-in-law and adoptive father. She appears on seals alongside Suppiluliuma; after her death, around 1345 BC, Henti became tawananna.

personas/nikal-mati/resumen.texto: Wife of the great king Tudhaliya II (or Tudhaliya I), sometimes considered the first of the Hittite queens with a Hurrian name. A ritual against magic protects her, together with her husband and children, from her sister-in-law Ziplantawiya; her daughter Asmunikal married Arnuwanda I.

personas/asmunikal/resumen.texto: Great queen of Hatti around 1385 BC, wife of Arnuwanda I and mother of Tudhaliya III; probably daughter of Tudhaliya II and Nikal-mati. She appears alongside her husband in administrative documents and oaths, prayed with him before the Kaska invasion, and some decrees were issued in her name alone.

personas/kuzi-teshub/resumen.texto: King of Karkemish c. 1180-1150 BC, son of Talmi-Teshub, the last Hittite viceroy in that city, and a descendant of Suppiluliuma I. He styled himself great king, which suggests that the dynasty of Hattusa had already fallen; he is known from seals from Lidar Höyük and from the inscriptions of his grandsons at Melid.

hechos/tumbas-reales-de-alaca-hoyuk/resu.texto: Fourteen shaft tombs of the Early Bronze Age at Alaca Höyük, with gold fibulae, diadems and figurines, bronze standards, and bull heads and legs. They are contemporary with the royal tombs of Ur and with Troy II.

hechos/palacio-de-uruk-en-arslantepe/res.texto: In the Late Chalcolithic, contemporary with Uruk, Arslantepe had a set of monumental buildings, among them two temples. Their exact function is uncertain.

hechos/destruccion-de-arslantepe-via/res.texto: Around 3000 BC the complex of Arslantepe was burned and destroyed, with many small objects left in place. Afterwards Kura-Araxes pottery appears.

hechos/enclave-de-uruk-en-hacinebi/resum.texto: At Hacınebi Tepe, by a crossing of the Euphrates, an enclave of the Uruk culture was established among a local population. The only Uruk bulla recovered in Turkey was found there, with tokens and two cylinder seals.

hechos/troya-i/titulo.texto: Founding of the Citadel of Troy I

hechos/troya-i/resumen.texto: Troy I was a small citadel of less than a hectare, with strong limestone walls, on the shore of a lagoon. A fire destroyed it around 2550 BC.

hechos/troya-ii/titulo.texto: Troy II and the So-Called Treasure of Priam

hechos/troya-ii/resumen.texto: Troy II, c. 2550-2300 BC, had a divided citadel, a lower town and megaron-type buildings. In 1873 Schliemann found there a set of jewels and gold objects that he called the «Treasure of Priam», although the layer is a thousand years older than the Mycenaean period.

hechos/destruccion-de-troya-ii/resumen.texto: Troy II was destroyed twice; the last time around 2300 BC. There is no proof that it was an attack, although it has been linked to a wider crisis at several sites in the Near East.

hechos/fundacion-de-troya-vi/resumen.texto: Troy VI, c. 1750-1300 BC, was a citadel city on terraces with ashlar walls. The lower town, discovered at the end of the 1980s by Manfred Korfmann's excavations, showed that the city was much larger than believed; its extent of about 30 ha is a debated estimate.

hechos/destruccion-de-troya-vi/resumen.texto: The Troy VIh layer was destroyed around 1300 BC, with fallen walls and collapses pointing to an earthquake, although a revolt or an attack has also been proposed. The inhabitants rebuilt the city as Troy VIIa.

hechos/expansion-de-kura-araxes/resumen.texto: The Kura-Araxes culture, which some date between c. 4000 and 2000 BC and others narrow according to site, appeared on the Ararat plain, and by about 3000 BC it extended north of the Caucasus. It covered Armenia, eastern Georgia, Azerbaijan, northwestern Iran and eastern Turkey.

hechos/cultura-de-maikop/resumen.texto: The Maykop culture of the western Caucasus, c. 3700 to 3000 BC, is known from its mounds with more than 7000 gold objects and 1000 silver ones, and from solid wheels from the Novokorsunskaya finds. Its link with the Yamnaya culture is debated; genetic data from 2018 derive it from farmers of western Georgia.

hechos/cultura-de-trialeti-vanadzor/resu.texto: Culture of the southern Caucasus between the late 3rd and early 2nd millennium BC, with elite mounds of four-wheeled chariots and gold objects. It arose where Kura-Araxes had been and developed into the Lchashen-Metsamor culture.

hechos/cultura-de-lchashen-metsamor/resu.texto: Late Bronze and early Iron Age culture (c. 1500-700 BC) of the southern Caucasus, especially Armenia, with fluted pottery and cyclopean fortresses. It is associated with the Etiuni tribal league of the Urartian inscriptions.

hechos/pithana-toma-nesa/resumen.texto: According to the Anitta text, Pithana, king of Kussara, took Neša (Kanesh) “at night, by force”, without harming its inhabitants. The date is approximate and the location of Kussara is unresolved.

hechos/incursion-de-uhna-de-zalpuwa-sobr.texto: King Uhna of Zalpuwa sacked Kanesh and carried off the city's idol of the god Siu, according to the Anitta text. The date of 1833 BC is approximate, and some see it as the cause of the fire of level II of the karum.

hechos/destruccion-del-karum-nivel-ii/ti.texto: Fire of the Kanesh Karum, Level II

hechos/destruccion-del-karum-nivel-ii/re.texto: Level II of the Kanesh karum, c. 1974-1836 BC (middle chronology according to Veenhof), ended in a fire. It is attributed either to a conquest of Assur by the kings of Eshnunna or, according to Bryce, to Uhna's raid.

hechos/palacio-de-warshama-en-kanesh/res.texto: Dendrochronology dates much of the timber of the palace of Warshama in the city of Kanesh to 1832 BC, with repairs until 1779 BC. According to one chronology, Warshama governed Kanesh c. 1775-1750 BC.

hechos/refundacion-del-karum-nivel-ib/ti.texto: Reconstruction of the Kanesh Karum, Level Ib

hechos/refundacion-del-karum-nivel-ib/re.texto: After a period of abandonment, Kanesh was rebuilt on its ruins and became a prosperous trading center again, c. 1798 to 1740 BC. Its trade depended on Ishme-Dagan I, son of Shamshi-Adad I, who ruled Assur.

hechos/anitta-recupera-el-idolo-de-zalpu.texto: Anitta put down the revolt of Neša, made it his capital, invaded Zalpuwa, captured its king Huzziya and recovered the idol of Siu. The date is approximate.

hechos/anitta-destruye-hattusa/titulo.texto: Anitta Destroys Hattusa and Curses It

hechos/anitta-destruye-hattusa/resumen.texto: A layer of ash at Hattusa is linked to its destruction by Anitta, who according to his text cursed it and caused its king Piyusti to be defeated. The curse did not prevent it from later becoming the Hittite capital. It is dated to around 1725 BC according to Anitta's reign; other dates put it around 1700 BC.

hechos/destruccion-del-karum-nivel-ib/ti.texto: Fire of the Kanesh Karum, Level Ib

hechos/destruccion-del-karum-nivel-ib/re.texto: The karum of Kanesh burned again at the end of level Ib, with many merchants' goods left behind. It was attributed to the fall of Assur or to attacks by neighboring kings and by Hammurabi of Babylon; other dates put it around 1710-1705 BC.

hechos/destruccion-de-beycesultan/titulo.texto: Destruction of the Palace of Beycesultan

hechos/destruccion-de-beycesultan/resume.texto: The palace of Beycesultan, similar in plan to that of Knossos, was abandoned and burned around 1700 BC. Mellaart attributed this to Hattusili I in his war against Arzawa; this is not certain.

hechos/traslado-de-la-capital-a-hattusa/.texto: Hattusili I Moves the Capital to Hattusa
A king called Labarna changed his name to Hattusili (“the one of Hattusa”) and moved the capital from Neša to Hattusa around 1650 BC (middle chronology). This step is attributed to Hattusili I.

hechos/campanas-de-hattusili-i/titulo.texto: Campaigns of Hattusili I in Anatolia and Syria

hechos/campanas-de-hattusili-i/resumen.texto: The annals of Hattusili I recount five years of campaigns: Zalpa and Sanahuitta (year 1), Alalakh and other cities of Syria (year 2), Arzawa (year 3), the capture of Sanahuitta after a five-month siege (year 4), and the crossing of the Euphrates (year 5). They survive in a later copy.

hechos/hattusili-i-ataca-arzawa/resumen.texto: In his third year Hattusili I went to the land of Arzawa and carried off its livestock, according to his annals. It is the oldest mention of Arzawa, then written Arzawiya; the place is the kingdom's later capital.

hechos/hattusili-i-cruza-el-eufrates/res.texto: In the fifth and last year of the campaign, Hattusili I crossed the Euphrates, something that according to his annals only Sargon of Akkad had done, in the opposite direction, and he conquered a long list of lands.

hechos/reintroduccion-del-cuneiforme-en-.texto: Reintroduction of Cuneiform Writing in Anatolia

After the end of the karum, cuneiform ceased to be used in Anatolia. It has been suggested that Hattusili I reintroduced it on his return from Syria with captured scribes, a point that Kloekhorst disputes.

hechos/leyes-hititas-compiladas/resumen.texto: The Hittite laws, c. 1650-1500 BC, set penalties for assault, theft, witchcraft and divorce, and include humane treatment of slaves. They were copied in Old, Middle and Late Hittite, which indicates that they remained in force throughout the empire.

hechos/asesinato-de-mursili-i/resumen.texto: Hantili, cupbearer of Mursili I and husband of his sister, killed him with the help of his son-in-law Zidanta and seized the throne. According to the Edict of Telipinu, this began a series of murders that weakened the kingdom.

hechos/kizzuwatna-se-independiza-bajo-am.texto: Kizzuwatna Breaks Away from the Hittite Kingdom

Under Ammuna, Adaniya in Cilicia rebelled and from then on was called Kizzuwatna, and it grew northward to the Anti-Taurus. The Hurrians took advantage of Hittite dynastic struggles to gain influence.

hechos/tratado-de-telipinu-con-isputahsu.texto: Telipinu Makes a Pact with Isputahsu of Kizzuwatna
Telipinu signed a treaty with Isputahsu, king of Kizzuwatna, allying with that kingdom against a rival Hurrian state. With that alliance he recovered some ground.

hechos/edicto-de-telipinu-hecho/resumen.texto: Telipinu had an edict written recounting the history of the crimes of the Hittite court and establishing a rule of succession to prevent further murders. Its text makes it possible to reconstruct the sequence of kings of the Old Kingdom.

hechos/tratado-de-zidanta-ii-con-pilliya.texto: Treaty of Zidanta II with Pilliya of Kizzuwatna

Zidanta II signed with Pilliya, king of Kizzuwatna, a treaty between equals, the last of its kind before Kizzuwatna lost its independence. Pilliya, a vassal of Mitanni, also made a pact with Idrimi of Alalakh.

hechos/tratado-de-sunassura-hecho/titulo.texto: Tudhaliya I/II and the Treaty of Sunassura

hechos/tratado-de-sunassura-hecho/resume.texto: Sunassura of Kizzuwatna signed with Tudhaliya I/II a treaty of subordination. It marked the end of Kizzuwatna's independence, which was then integrated into the Hittite kingdom.

hechos/ataques-de-attarsiya-a-madduwatta.texto: According to the accusation against Madduwatta, the Ahhiyawan chief Attarsiya attacked him twice and forced him to flee, the second time with 100 chariots and 1000 soldiers. Tudhaliya I/II installed him at Zippasla, and a Hittite army restored him. The site of the fighting is unknown, so the capital of Arzawa is used as its marker.

hechos/madduwatta-invade-arzawa/resumen.texto: Despite the prohibition of Tudhaliya I/II, Madduwatta attacked Arzawa, then ruled by a Kupanta-Kurunta of Arzawa, distinct from the later king of Mira, and failed; the Hittites had to come to his aid. Later he allied with Kupanta-Kurunta and Attarsiya, and attacked Alashiya with them.

hechos/sometimiento-de-assuwa/titulo.texto: Tudhaliya I/II Defeats the Assuwa League

hechos/sometimiento-de-assuwa/lugar.texto: Western Anatolia (Assuwa region; no precise site)

hechos/sometimiento-de-assuwa/resumen.texto: The confederation of 22 states of Assuwa, in western Anatolia, formed against the Hittites and was defeated by Tudhaliya I/II around 1420 BC. Its name is thought to have given rise to the name Asia.

hechos/kaskas-saquean-ciudades-hititas/t.texto: The Kaska Sack Hittite Cities Tapikka, Sarissa and Sapinuwa

hechos/kaskas-saquean-ciudades-hititas/r.texto: Under Arnuwanda I, the Kaska plundered Hittite holy cities, among them Tapikka, Sarissa and Sapinuwa, and reached about 100 km from Hattusa. Arnuwanda partly drove them out and tried to buy their peace.

hechos/guerras-de-supervivencia-hititas/.texto: A series of wars between the Hittites and Arzawa, the Kaska and Hayasa-Azzi, between c. 1400 and 1350 BC. Hattusa was sacked or abandoned, and the court withdrew to Samuha, from where Tudhaliya III and Suppiluliuma I reconquered the lost lands.

hechos/la-corte-hitita-se-retira-a-samuh.texto: The Hittite Court Withdraws to Samuha
From Sapinuwa, the court of Tudhaliya III moved to Samuha, which served as his base for counterattacks. Samuha was the temporary capital until Hattusa was retaken.

hechos/diplomacia-egipcia-con-arzawa/tit.texto: Amenhotep III Writes to Tarhuntaradu of Arzawa

hechos/diplomacia-egipcia-con-arzawa/res.texto: Amenhotep III proposed a diplomatic marriage to Tarhuntaradu of Arzawa and said he had heard that Hattusa was paralyzed. Letters EA 31 and 32 were written in Hittite, because Arzawa had no Akkadian scribes.

hechos/asesinato-de-tudhaliya-el-joven/t.texto: Suppiluliuma I Murders Tudhaliya the Younger

hechos/asesinato-de-tudhaliya-el-joven/r.texto: On the death of Tudhaliya III, Suppiluliuma I and his supporters killed the heir Tudhaliya the Younger and some brothers. An oracle later saw in that crime a cause of the plague.

hechos/tushratta-asciende-al-trono-de-mi.texto: Tushratta Ascends the Throne of Mitanni

Artashumara, who succeeded his father Shuttarna II, was murdered by a pro-Hittite group led by Tuhi, who put Tushratta on the throne and declared himself regent. Tushratta, who was young, had Tuhi executed.

hechos/guerra-de-un-ano/titulo.texto: Suppiluliuma I's One-Year War Against Mitanni

hechos/guerra-de-un-ano/resumen.texto: Suppiluliuma I invaded Mitanni, sacked Waššukanni and crossed the Euphrates; what he conquered in Syria west of the river is told in the account of the Hittite conquest of western Syria. The date of 1345 BC is approximate; Tushratta fled.

hechos/toma-de-karkemish/resumen.texto: After a siege, Suppiluliuma I took Karkemish, which was still in Mitanni's hands, and placed his son Piyassili there as king. With that, the viceroys of Karkemish and Aleppo governed Syria in his name.

hechos/plaga-hitita/resumen.texto: An epidemic affected the Hittites for about twenty years and killed Suppiluliuma I and Arnuwanda II. Mursili II attributed it to Egyptian prisoners brought to Hattusa and, in his prayers, to the sins of his father; it has been proposed that it was tularemia.

hechos/tushratta-asesinado-por-su-hijo/r.texto: According to the Hittite treaty with Shattiwaza, one of Tushratta's sons killed him, and Shuttarna III and the Assyrians contested the kingdom with Artatama II. This is known only from the Hittite account.

hechos/shattiwaza-vasallo-de-suppilulium.texto: Shattiwaza, son of Tushratta, fled to Babylon and then to Hatti, where Suppiluliuma I gave him a daughter and made him swear vassalage. It is the only testimony to his reign.

hechos/shattiwaza-recupera-mitani/titulo.texto: The Hittite Army Restores Shattiwaza to Mitanni

hechos/shattiwaza-recupera-mitani/resume.texto: Piyassili and Shattiwaza crossed the Euphrates at Karkemish, took Irridu and Harran, and moved on to Waššukanni; Shattiwaza reigned over what remained of Mitanni, which the Assyrians called Hanigalbat.

hechos/dioses-indoarios-en-el-tratado-de.texto: Indo-Aryan Gods in the Treaty of Shattiwaza

The treaty cites as guarantors Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya, gods who also appear in Vedic texts. The Indo-Aryan terms of Mitanni, in the names of kings and gods and in horse terminology, are explained by an Indo-Aryan elite group.

hechos/texto-de-kikkuli-hecho/titulo.texto: Kikkuli Writes His Horse Training Text

hechos/texto-de-kikkuli-hecho/resumen.texto: The horse trainer Kikkuli of Mitanni left a treatise of 1080 lines on training chariot horses, written mostly in Hittite. It contains Indo-Aryan terms.

hechos/murallas-de-hattusa/resumen.texto: Suppiluliuma I is credited with building the great wall of Hattusa, which encircles both the upper and the lower city. At its peak the city covered 1.8 km².

hechos/shaushtatar-saquea-assur/resumen.texto: A later Hittite text says that Shaushtatar carried the silver and gold doors of the palace of Assur to Washukanni, under King Nur-ili. Assyria is said to have paid tribute to Mitanni until Eriba-Adad I.

hechos/mursili-ii-ataca-arzawa/titulo.texto: Mursili II Defeats Uhha-Ziti of Arzawa

hechos/mursili-ii-ataca-arzawa/resumen.texto: According to the annals, Mursili II invaded Arzawa, and a lightning bolt struck Uhha-Ziti at Apasa; his son Piyama-Kurunta lost the battle of Walma on the Astarpa River, and Uhha-Ziti fled to islands under Ahhiyawa. Manapa-Tarhunta was pardoned.

hechos/mursili-ii-en-millawanda/resumen.texto: After the defeat of Arzawa, the city of Millawanda (Miletus) was affected and probably burned by the Hittites, because of Mycenaean support for Arzawa, although the Mycenaeans kept control of it.

hechos/batalla-de-ganuvara-hecho/lugar.texto: Armenian highlands (Hayasa-Azzi area; no precise site)

hechos/batalla-de-ganuvara-hecho/resumen.texto: While Mursili II was away, Nuvanza defeated 10,000 men and 700 chariots of Hayasa-Azzi, which were besieging Ganuvara. The following year Mursili invaded Hayasa, and in his eleventh year he received its submission.

hechos/eclipse-de-mursili/titulo.texto: Eclipse in the Tenth Year of Mursili II

hechos/eclipse-de-mursili/resumen.texto: The annals say that in the tenth year of Mursili II “the sun gave a sign” as he was about to attack Hayasa-Azzi. It is identified with a solar eclipse, and opinion is divided between that of 24 June 1312 BC (followed by Kuhrt and Bryce) and that of 13 April 1308 BC (followed by Freu).

hechos/instalacion-de-kupanta-kurunta-en.texto: Mursili II Places Kupanta-Kurunta on the Throne of Mira
Two years after the eclipse, Mira rebelled and Mursili II subdued it, sent Mashuiluwa into priesthood, and placed Kupanta-Kurunta on the throne.

hechos/traslado-de-la-capital-a-tarhunta.texto: Muwatalli II Moves the Capital to Tarhuntassa
Tarhuntassa (unidentified site; approximate location per Wikidata)

At the beginning of the 13th century BC, Muwatalli II moved the capital from Hattusa to Tarhuntassa. This has been explained by a military strategy against Egypt, by a religious reform (Singer), or by the city's position. The location of Tarhuntassa is not known; Türkmen-Karahöyük is a proposal from 2019.

hechos/tratado-de-alaksandu-hecho/titulo.texto: Treaty of Muwatalli II with Alaksandu of Wilusa

hechos/tratado-de-alaksandu-hecho/resume.texto: Muwatalli II confirmed Alaksandu as king of Wilusa, whom most identify with Troy (Hisarlık), and recalled three centuries of friendship between Hatti and Wilusa since Hattusili I. If it is Greek, his name would be the oldest attested form of Alexandros.

hechos/guerra-civil-de-hattusili-iii-con.texto: Hattusili III Deposes His Nephew Mursili III

Mursili III (Urhi-Teshub) had reassigned Nerik, and Hattusili III, who governed the north, rebelled, won a brief civil war and made himself king. His Apology justifies the coup as the order of the goddess Ishtar.

hechos/matrimonio-de-hattusili-iii-y-pud.texto: Hattusili III met and married Puduhepa, daughter of Pentipsarri, priest of Sauska, at Lawazantiya. She promoted the cults of Kizzuwatna and later became great queen.

hechos/disputa-hitita-con-ahhiyawa-por-w.texto: Hittites and Ahhiyawa Clash over Wilusa

A Hittite king writes to the king of Ahhiyawa that the two had been at odds over Wilusa (which most identify with Troy) and had made peace. An ambiguous verb can indicate anything from an exchange of hostile letters to a war.

hechos/rebeliones-de-piyamaradu/resumen.texto: For about 35 years Piyamaradu attacked the Hittite vassals of Arzawa, Seha, Lazpa and Wilusa, fled to Ahhiyawan territory, and married his daughter to Atpa, governor of Millawanda. Kings Muwatalli II, Hattusili III and Tudhaliya IV had to confront him.

hechos/deposicion-de-walmu/resumen.texto: The Milawata letter says that Walmu, king of Wilusa (which most identify with Troy, Hisarlık), was deposed, and asks for the claimant to be handed over to a Hittite envoy so that he can be restored. It does not say who deposed him.

hechos/tudhaliya-iv-construye-presas/tit.texto: Tudhaliya IV Builds Dams Against Drought

hechos/tudhaliya-iv-construye-presas/res.texto: Faced with a drought, Tudhaliya IV had at least 13 dams built to secure water; one of them survives, the Gölpınar dam, next to Alaca Höyük.

hechos/tratado-de-tudhaliya-iv-con-kurun.texto: Tudhaliya IV Renews Kurunta in Tarhuntassa

Tudhaliya IV confirmed his cousin Kurunta as king of Tarhuntassa in a treaty engraved on bronze, which fixes the borders of the kingdom. It has been proposed that Kurunta came to call himself great king.

hechos/ampliacion-de-yazilikaya/titulo.texto: Works of Tudhaliya IV at Yazılıkaya

hechos/ampliacion-de-yazilikaya/resumen.texto: The reliefs of the Yazılıkaya sanctuary, in use since the 16th century BC, mostly date from the reigns of Tudhaliya IV and Suppiluliuma II, when it was restored.

hechos/envio-de-trigo-a-hatti/titulo.texto: Famine and Wheat Shipments to Hatti

hechos/envio-de-trigo-a-hatti/resumen.texto: 13th-century BC texts mention urgent shipments of wheat from Merneptah of Egypt and from Mukish to Hatti, which suggests a famine in Anatolia or the eastern Mediterranean.

hechos/suppiluliuma-ii-saquea-tarhuntass.texto: Suppiluliuma II Conquers the Southwest and Tarhuntassa
Tarhuntassa (unidentified site; approximate location per Wikidata)

The Luwian inscriptions from Hattusa say that Suppiluliuma II took Wiyanawanda, Tamina, Masa, Lukka and Ikuna, and then defeated, sacked and annexed Tarhuntassa. It had been proposed that Hartapu, son of a Mursili, was the rival of Tarhuntassa; recent dating of his inscriptions places them in the 8th century BC.

hechos/abandono-de-hattusa/resumen.texto: Hattusa was gradually abandoned around 1190 BC (other sources put its destruction around 1200 BC), with the elites and the administration gone before parts of the city were burned. The destruction has been attributed to the Kaska, Phrygians and Brygians, but there is no conclusive proof; drought and a move of the court to the southwest have been proposed.

hechos/hattusili-i-saquea-zalpa/resumen.texto: In the first year of the campaign, according to his annals, Hattusili I reached Zalpa and Sanahuitta; he sacked Zalpa but could not take Sanahuitta. In 2020 it was proposed to identify this Zalpa, the one on the Euphrates or the Amanus, with Tilmen Höyük; another Zalpuwa, on the Black Sea, is the one in the Anitta text.

hechos/destruccion-del-complejo-de-zinci.texto: Destruction of the Monumental Complex at Zincirli
Complex DD at Zincirli, of the Middle Bronze II, was destroyed between 1632 and 1610 BC according to ten radiocarbon dates, perhaps by Hattusili I in his war against Zalpa.

hechos/incendio-de-kilise-tepe/resumen.texto: The settlement of Kilise Tepe was burned at the end of the 13th century BC, which some excavators attribute to the Sea Peoples. It was later rebuilt.

hechos/destruccion-de-alisar-hoyuk/resum.texto: Stratum IV of Alişar Hüyük, from the end of the Hittite empire, ended around 1200 BC in a widespread destruction. The site was little occupied until the Phrygian period.

hechos/destruccion-de-sarissa/resumen.texto: Sarissa was sacked, like other Hittite cities, around 1200 BC, and was later reoccupied and repaired before being abandoned. The imperial stratum was lost in a fire in the second half of the 13th century BC.

hechos/retorno-de-la-capital-a-hattusa/t.texto: Mursili III Returns the Capital to Hattusa

hechos/retorno-de-la-capital-a-hattusa/r.texto: Mursili III, son of Muwatalli II, moved the capital back to Hattusa shortly after coming to the throne.

hechos/matrimonio-de-suppiluliuma-i-con-.texto: Suppiluliuma I Marries a Babylonian Princess

Suppiluliuma I allied himself with Kassite Babylonia and married a Babylonian princess, possibly named Malnigal, who was his last queen and Tawananna. Mursili II later demoted and exiled her. The date is approximate.

hechos/tratado-de-suppiluliuma-i-con-huk.texto: Treaty of Suppiluliuma I with Hukkana of Hayasa
Suppiluliuma I gave his sister in marriage to Hukkana and made him king of Azzi-Hayasa in a treaty with extensive moral clauses. It was probably concluded at the beginning of his reign.

hechos/reconquista-de-nerik/resumen.texto: While serving as governor for his brother Muwatalli II, Hattusili III recovered the holy city of Nerik and rebuilt it as its chief priest. He named his firstborn Nerikkaili after it.

hechos/estandartes-de-alaca-hoyuk/resume.texto: In the tombs of Alaca Höyük were found copper standards shaped like bulls or deer on pedestals, and openwork discs with crosses. Their function is still debated.

hechos/envio-de-la-estatua-de-sauska-a-e.texto: Tushratta Sends the Statue of Shaushka to Egypt
With Amenhotep III ill, Tushratta sent to Egypt the statue of the goddess Shaushka of Nineveh, as Shuttarna II had done before. Letter EA 23 recounts it.

hechos/kurganes-de-martkopi/resumen.texto: The rich kurgans of Martkopi, in eastern Georgia, belong to the initial phase of the early kurgans of central Transcaucasia and are almost contemporary with the first mounds of Trialeti.

hechos/tumba-real-de-arslantepe/resumen.texto: At the beginning of the 3rd millennium BC a large cist tomb was built at Arslantepe among modest buildings. Its architecture and metallurgy have been linked to the Maykop-Novosvobodnaya kurgans, although the chronology and sequence are not settled.

hechos/isuwa-ataca-kizzuwatna/resumen.texto: In the concentric invasions against Tudhaliya III, Isuwa attacked and sacked Kizzuwatna, while Arzawa took much of western Hittite territory. Later Hittite texts present this as a coordinated conspiracy, which modern specialists consider unlikely.

hechos/arzawa-conquista-el-oeste-hitita/.texto: Around 1370 BC, under Tudhaliya III, Arzawa conquered much of western Anatolia and the Lower Land, lands that the Hittites had never lost. Suppiluliuma I later recovered them.

hechos/fiesta-de-puruli/resumen.texto: The Hittites kept the Hattian spring festival of Puruli in honor of the storm god of Nerik, at which the myth of the death of Illuyanka was recited. It continued after Hattusili I took Nerik.

hechos/hayasa-azzi-toma-samuha/resumen.texto: During the wars of survival, Hayasa-Azzi took Samuha, the city that served as the base of the Hittite court. Tudhaliya III sent his son Suppiluliuma, who defeated Hayasa-Azzi and made it a vassal.

hechos/suppiluliuma-i-recupera-tuwanuwa/.texto: Under Tudhaliya III, Suppiluliuma I defeated Arzawa in several battles and recovered Tuwanuwa, probably Tyana, which the enemy occupied. According to Mursili II, bringing order to the west took him about twenty years.

hechos/suppiluliuma-i-conquista-melid/re.texto: Melid, regional capital of Isuwa on the Hittite-Mitanni frontier and loyal to Tushratta, fell to Suppiluliuma I around 1350 BC. Suppiluliuma used it as a base in his campaign against Waššukanni.

hechos/troya-iii-a-v/resumen.texto: Between 2300 and 1750 BC Troy remained occupied in three little-known layers, because Schliemann destroyed its remains without recording them. Troy IV (c. 2000-1820 BC) has beehive ovens and mudbrick houses, and Troy V (c. 1820-1750 BC) had imported Minoan objects.

hechos/santuario-de-metsamor/resumen.texto: In the Late Bronze and Early Iron Age (15th-8th centuries BC) Metsamor was a religious and economic center, with a complex of five small temples with clay altars on the southern slope. It had metalworking and gold necklaces.

hechos/kirta-funda-la-dinastia-de-mitani.texto: Kirta, Traditional Founder of the Mitanni Dynasty

Tradition makes Kirta, a semi-legendary Hurrian king, the founder of the Mitanni dynasty around 1540 BC (some put it nearer 1500 BC). Epigraphic support is scarce: a seal found at Alalakh names Shuttarna as son of Kirta, king of Maitani.

hechos/reconquista-de-kizzuwatna-por-sup.texto: At the beginning of his reign Suppiluliuma I reconquered Kizzuwatna, which had been under indirect Mitanni control. Kizzuwatna rebelled during his reign, but it remained within the Hittite empire for about 200 years.

hechos/invasion-de-cilicia-por-los-puebl.texto: Sea Peoples Displace the Inhabitants of Cilicia

Around 1200 BC an invasion by the Sea Peoples may have temporarily displaced the inhabitants of the Cilician plain. After the fall of Hattusa, the Neo-Hittite kingdom of Quwe emerged in the former territory of Kizzuwatna.

hechos/madduwatta-recibe-asilo-hitita/ti.texto: Tudhaliya I/II Grants Asylum to Madduwatta

hechos/madduwatta-recibe-asilo-hitita/re.texto: Attacked by the Ahhiyawan chief Attarsiya, Madduwatta fled and obtained asylum from the Hittite king Tudhaliya I/II, who installed him as ruler of Zippasla and of the Land of the Siyanta River, in exchange for an oath of loyalty and of having no foreign relations of his own.

hechos/madduwatta-y-attarsiya-atacan-ala.texto: According to the indictment, Madduwatta joined with Attarsiya to raid the island of Alashiya, which the Hittites considered theirs. Madduwatta claimed that no one had informed him of that claim.

hechos/madduwatta-toma-hapalla/titulo.texto: Madduwatta Occupies Hapalla and Returns It to Arnuwanda I

hechos/madduwatta-toma-hapalla/resumen.texto: Arnuwanda I assigned his vassal Madduwatta to help in Hapalla against a local uprising, and Madduwatta kept the country. Under threats from Arnuwanda, he returned it to the Hittites.

hechos/acusacion-contra-madduwatta-hecho.texto: The Indictment of Madduwatta Is Drawn Up

The text, written under Arnuwanda I, reviews Madduwatta's violations of the treaty from the reign of Tudhaliya I/II onward, and contains the first mention of Ahhiyawa (“Ahhiya”) and the name of Attarissiya. It is not known whether it was a legal document or a diplomatic warning; the surviving copy looks like a draft, and Madduwatta's fate is unknown.

hechos/suppiluliuma-i-incendia-hapalla/r.texto: On reconquering the Hittite lands, Suppiluliuma I sent his army to Hapalla, whose capital was burned and whose inhabitants were deported.

hechos/mursili-ii-reinstala-a-targasnall.texto: Mursili II Reinstates Targasnalli in Hapalla

After the failure of Uhha-Ziti's rebellion, Targasnalli, the first known ruler of Hapalla, submitted again to Hattusa, and the Hittites restored him to the throne. The treaty with Kupanta-Kurunta shows him still reigning around 1310 BC.

hechos/uhha-ziti-se-rebela-contra-mursil.texto: Uhha-Ziti of Arzawa Rebels Against the Hittites

From Apasa, Uhha-Ziti rebelled and took in refugees from Attarimma, Huwarsanassa and Suruda. As Mursili II marched toward Arzawa, a meteorite fell on Apasa and wounded Uhha-Ziti, who made an alliance with the king of Ahhiyuwa.

hechos/piyama-kurunta-ataca-mira/resumen.texto: Uhha-Ziti ordered his son Piyama-Kurunta to attack Mira, whose king Mashuiluwa was married to a sister of Mursili II. He attacked and possibly destroyed the city of Impa, but the army of Mira drove him back.

hechos/batalla-de-walma-en-el-rio-astarp.texto: Battle of Walma, on the Astarpa River

In the third year of Mursili II, Piyama-Kurunta, sent by his ailing father, faced him at Walma, by the Astarpa River, and was defeated. The treaty of Mursili II with Kupanta-Kurunta fixes the Astarpa as the boundary of Kuwaliya; it is probably identified with the Maeander, and the site of Walma is unknown.

hechos/toma-de-apasa-y-asedio-de-puranda.texto: Mursili II Takes Apasa and Besieges Puranda
Mursili II entered Apasa, apparently without a battle, and the refugees fled to Puranda. Uhha-Ziti died during the siege, and Piyama-Kurunta surrendered and was deported to Hattusa.

hechos/mursili-ii-asedia-seha/titulo.texto: Mursili II Besieges the Capital of Seha

hechos/mursili-ii-asedia-seha/resumen.texto: According to the annals, Mursili II besieged the capital of the Land of the Seha River and was about to destroy it when, at its gates, he accepted the plea of the mother of King Manapa-Tarhunta.

hechos/tratado-de-mursili-ii-con-manapa-.texto: Treaty of Mursili II with Manapa-Tarhunta
The treaty confirmed Manapa-Tarhunta as a Hittite vassal of the Land of the Seha River, after the revolt in which he had taken part.

hechos/carta-de-manapa-tarhunta-hecho/ti.texto: Manapa-Tarhunta Writes to the Hittite King

hechos/carta-de-manapa-tarhunta-hecho/re.texto: Letter from Manapa-Tarhunta, probably to Muwatalli II: he reports that Hittite troops reached Seha and went on to attack Wilusa, and that Piyamaradu had installed Atpa in Seha. It recounts the desertion of dyers from Lazpa, whose return Kupanta-Kurunta of Mira negotiated.

hechos/muwatalli-ii-instala-a-masturi-en.texto: Muwatalli II Installs Masturi in Seha
Manapa-Tarhunta was deposed and replaced by Masturi, who may have been his son, with the support of Muwatalli II. Seha remained loyal to the Hittites during his reign.

hechos/tudhaliya-iv-sofoca-la-revuelta-d.texto: Tudhaliya IV Puts Down the Revolt in Seha
Tarhunta-Radu deposed Masturi, apparently with the support of the Ahhiyawa. Tudhaliya IV crushed the revolt and restored to the throne a descendant of Manapa-Tarhunta.

hechos/carta-de-milawata-hecho/titulo.texto: Letter from a Hittite King to a Vassal on the West Coast

hechos/carta-de-milawata-hecho/resumen.texto: The letter requires the addressee to settle a dispute over hostages, to hand over fugitives, and to surrender a claimant to the throne of Wilusa so that the Hittites can restore him as king. Bryce and Burney attribute it to Tudhaliya IV, addressed to a later king of Mira, probably Tarkasnawa.

hechos/carta-de-tawagalawa-hecho/titulo.texto: Letter from the Hittite King to the King of Ahhiyawa

hechos/carta-de-tawagalawa-hecho/resumen.texto: The author, generally identified as Hattusili III (some propose Muwatalli II), asks for cooperation against the warlord Piyamaradu, who has taken refuge in Ahhiyawan territory, and proposes either extraditing him, expelling him, or granting him asylum on conditions. He addresses the king of Ahhiyawa as “brother” and recalls a past hostility over Wilusa, now settled.

hechos/matrimonio-de-mashuiluwa-y-muwatt.texto: Suppiluliuma I Marries Mashuiluwa to Muwatti and Restores Him in Mira

Suppiluliuma I married his daughter Muwatti, sister of Mursili II, to Mashuiluwa, king of Mira-Kuwaliya, who came from the lands of Arzawa, and restored him to the throne after a coup by other nobles. Mashuiluwa remained a Hittite vassal in Mira.

hechos/mira-apoya-a-urhi-teshub/titulo.texto: Mira Supports Urhi-Teshub Against Hattusili III

hechos/mira-apoya-a-urhi-teshub/resumen.texto: During the reign of Hattusili III there were disagreements between the Hittites and the king of Mira, probably Kupanta-Kurunta, over his support for Urhi-Teshub, whom Hattusili had deposed. It is not clear whether there was war.

hechos/hattusili-iii-nombra-a-kurunta-re.texto: Hattusili III Names Kurunta King of Tarhuntassa
Tarhuntassa (unidentified site; approximate location per Wikidata)

After deposing Mursili III, Hattusili III named his nephew Kurunta, son of Muwatalli II, king of Tarhuntassa. Another treaty, that of Ulmi-Teshub, almost always names the king as Ulmi-Teshub, and some specialists think Ulmi-Teshub and Kurunta were two different rulers.

hechos/kaskas-ocupan-las-ruinas-de-nerik.texto: The Kaska Enter the Ruins of Nerik

The Kaska first appear in Hittite prayers from the reign of Hantili II, which mention their advance toward the ruins of the holy city of Nerik. Arnuwanda I later composed a prayer asking the gods to return Nerik to the kingdom; Hattusili III recovered it much later.

hechos/rebelion-de-ishupitta/resumen.texto: In the time of the ailing Arnuwanda II, the veteran Hannutti marched to Ishupitta, but died there. Ishupitta broke away from Hatti, and Mursili II recorded in his annals that he put down that rebellion.

hechos/pihhuniya-unifica-a-los-kaskas/re.texto: Pihhuniya of Tipiya, who according to Hittite texts “ruled like a king”, united the Kaska for the first time, conquered Istitina, and reached Zazzissa. Mursili II defeated him and took him prisoner to Hattusa.

hechos/kaskas-saquean-hattusa-bajo-muwat.texto: The Kaska Sack Hattusa Under Muwatalli II
At the beginning of the 13th century BC, during the reign of Muwatalli II, the Kaska sacked Hattusa. Muwatalli stopped recruiting them as troops and moved the capital to Tarhuntassa.

hechos/batalla-de-kumaha/titulo.texto: Battle of Kumaha Against Karanni of Hayasa

hechos/batalla-de-kumaha/lugar.texto: Armenian highlands (Hayasa-Azzi area; no precise site)

hechos/batalla-de-kumaha/resumen.texto: Tudhaliya III and Suppiluliuma I invaded Hayasa-Azzi and forced a battle with its king Karanni near Kumaha. The passage of the Deeds of Suppiluliuma that recounts the outcome is lost, but afterward Suppiluliuma made Hayasa a vassal by a treaty with Hukkana.

hechos/anniya-de-azzi-saquea-dankuwa/lug.texto: Armenian highlands (Hayasa-Azzi area; no precise site)

hechos/anniya-de-azzi-saquea-dankuwa/res.texto: In the seventh year of Mursili II, the “lord of Azzi” Anniya took advantage of Pihhuniya's unification of the Kaska, ravaged the Hittite border region of Dankuwa, and carried off its population.

hechos/mursili-ii-ataca-ura/titulo.texto: Mursili II Attacks the Fortress of Ura

hechos/mursili-ii-ataca-ura/lugar.texto: Armenian highlands (Hayasa-Azzi area; no precise site)

hechos/mursili-ii-ataca-ura/resumen.texto: Anniya refused to return the captives, and Mursili II attacked Ura, the border fortress of Hayasa. In the following spring he crossed the Euphrates and reorganized his army at Ingalova.

hechos/anzapahhadu-derrota-a-himuili/tit.texto: Anzapahhadu of Arzawa Defeats the General Himuili

hechos/anzapahhadu-derrota-a-himuili/res.texto: Around 1355 BC, during the Hittite reconquest, Anzapahhadu of Arzawa defeated the Hittite general Himuili, before submitting to a new invasion led by Suppiluliuma I himself.

hechos/la-capital-hitita-pasa-a-sapinuwa.texto: The Hittite Capital Moves to Sapinuwa
Faced with attacks by the Kaska, Hayasa-Azzi and other enemies, Tudhaliya III moved the court to Sapinuwa, from where he tried unsuccessfully to mount a counteroffensive.

hechos/espada-de-assuwa-en-hattusa/titul.texto: Sword of Assuwa Offered to the Storm God

hechos/espada-de-assuwa-en-hattusa/resum.texto: A sword of possibly Mycenaean style was found at Hattusa; its inscription suggests that it was taken from a soldier of Assuwa and left as an offering to the Hittite storm god. Eric Cline cites it among the signs of Ahhiyawan support for Assuwa.

hechos/tablilla-de-tutulla-en-inandiktep.texto: Land Grant to Tutulla Sealed with the Tabarna Seal

An Akkadian tablet from İnandıktepe records a land grant to the official Tutulla, sealed with the archaic tabarna seal, which names no king. Its use until the reigns of Telipinu and Alluwamna dates it to the late 16th century BC.

hechos/murallas-de-troya-vi-ampliadas/ti.texto: Expansion of the Walls of Troy VI

hechos/murallas-de-troya-vi-ampliadas/re.texto: The walls of the Troy VI citadel were renewed several times and went from 1.2 to 5 m thick around 1400 BC. Their “saw-tooth” segments of 7 to 10 m and their slope have parallels in Mycenaean citadels and in Hattusa.

hechos/troya-viia/titulo.texto: Rebuilding the Citadel as Troy VIIa

hechos/troya-viia/resumen.texto: After the destruction of Troy VI, probably by an earthquake, its inhabitants raised Troy VIIa reusing the walls, which they reinforced with stone towers, and filled the citadel with small houses and large buried jars.

hechos/troya-viib1/resumen.texto: After the destruction of Troy VIIa, the city was rebuilt as Troy VIIb1 on the old structures, with a smaller population and new hand-made pottery. A Luwian hieroglyphic seal was found there.

hechos/sello-luvita-de-troya-hecho/titul.texto: Luwian Hieroglyphic Seal from Troy VIIb1

hechos/sello-luvita-de-troya-hecho/resum.texto: A bronze seal with two faces bears the name of a woman on one side and, on the other, that of a man who was a scribe. It is the only evidence of pre-Classical writing at the site; the hypothesis of an itinerant scribe, or of a date earlier than the find context, is an attempt to explain why palace bureaucracies were no longer there.

hechos/cultura-colca/resumen.texto: Archaeological culture of the Bronze and Early Iron Age in western Georgia, with wooden houses, adaptation to wetlands, and bronze metallurgy with decorated axes, often in hoards. It moves from a Proto-Colchian phase to an Early Colchian one and is succeeded by Greek colonization.
