hechos/cultura-de-novosvobodnaya/resumen.texto: Early Bronze Age culture of the slopes of the northern Caucasus, named after the megalithic tombs of Novosvobodnaya. Nikolaev and Safronov distinguished it from the Maykop culture; Rezepkin saw ceramic similarities with the funnel beaker.

hechos/cultura-de-khojaly-gadabay/resume.texto: Late Bronze and Early Iron Age culture (roughly 13th to 7th centuries BC) of Karabakh, in the southern Caucasus, with sites at Khojaly, Gadabay and Ganja. Soviet archaeologists have excavated it since the 1920s.

hechos/puerta-de-la-esfinge-de-alaca-hoy.texto: The Sphinx Gate, flanked by stone reliefs, marked the entrance to the Hittite city of Alaca Höyük and is dated from the 14th century BC.

hechos/bulla-con-fichas-de-hacinebi/titu.texto: Bulla with Twelve Tokens from Hacınebi

hechos/bulla-con-fichas-de-hacinebi/resu.texto: At the Uruk enclave of Hacınebi a clay bulla was found, sealed with two cylinder seals, containing twelve proto-literate tokens (ten spheres and two discs); it is the only one recovered in Turkey. Radiocarbon dates place the arrival of the people of Uruk between 3700 and 3400 BC.

hechos/los-hatianos-en-anatolia-central/.texto: The Hattians, who spoke a language that was neither Semitic nor Indo-European, inhabited Hatti in central Anatolia from the Early Bronze Age; their main center was Hattusa. The Hittites, who spoke an Indo-European language, gradually absorbed them by about 1700 BC and kept the name of the land.

hechos/lengua-hatiana/resumen.texto: Hattic, an agglutinative non-Indo-European language, was spoken in the 2nd millennium BC between Hattusa and Nerik; the Hittites called it hattili. The archives of Hattusa and Sapinuwa preserve bilingual Hittite-Hattic texts.

hechos/primeros-testimonios-de-los-hurri.texto: Earliest Evidence of the Hurrians at Urkesh

The Hurrians are first documented at Urkesh: a seal from around 2300 BC names Tupkish, a king with a Hurrian name, and the first inscription in their language is from King Tish-atal, of the 21st century BC. They later occupied northern Syria, upper Mesopotamia and southeastern Anatolia, and their most important kingdom was Mitanni.

hechos/reino-de-mitani/resumen.texto: Mitanni, called Hanigalbat by the Assyrians and Naharin by the Egyptians, was a Hurrian-speaking kingdom of northern Syria and southeastern Anatolia, with Indo-Aryan influences. It reached Kizzuwatna to the west and Arrapha to the east, and no royal annals or chronicles of its own have been found: its history is known from what its neighbors say.

hechos/wilusa-en-los-textos-hititas/resu.texto: Wilusa was a city of western Anatolia in the Late Bronze Age, known from references in fragmentary Hittite records, and a Hittite vassal according to the treaty of Alaksandu. Most specialists identify it with Troy (Hisarlık), which links it with the legendary Trojan War; the identification remains debated.

hechos/lukka-en-los-textos-hititas-y-egi.texto: Lukka was a region of southwestern Anatolia, hostile according to Hittite and Egyptian texts, whose name is considered related to Lycia; its extent is debated (Bryce extends it to Lycaonia, Pisidia and Lycia, and Yakubovich limits it to Lycia). The Amarna letters mention Lukka raids against Alashiya around the middle of the 14th century BC, and Suppiluliuma II unsuccessfully tried to defeat them.

hechos/reino-de-arzawa/resumen.texto: Arzawa was a kingdom and confederation of states in western Anatolia; its main state had its capital at Apasa, and in the Hittite texts the confederation also included Mira, Hapalla, Wilusa and the Land of the Seha River. It had a turbulent relationship with the Hittites, sometimes allied with Ahhiyawa, and Egypt treated it as a great king in the Amarna period, until Mursili II subdued it around 1320 BC.

hechos/reino-de-kizzuwatna/resumen.texto: Kizzuwatna was a kingdom of the Cilician plain, attested in writing from the late 16th century BC and centered on Kummanni, whose location is uncertain (Sirkeli Höyük has been proposed). It lay between Hatti and Mitanni, came under Hittite control under Tudhaliya I/II, and Suppiluliuma I reconquered it.

hechos/primeras-inscripciones-en-jerogli.texto: The earliest secure inscriptions in Anatolian hieroglyphs, a script of some 500 signs that writes Luwian, date from the Late Bronze Age, the 14th and 13th centuries BC; before that they appear on seals that carry only names, titles and signs of good omen. After about two centuries of scarce evidence, the script was taken up again in the early Iron Age.

hechos/posible-toma-de-hattusa-por-kurun.texto: Kurunta and the Possible Capture of Hattusa

It has been proposed that Kurunta of Tarhuntassa briefly took Hattusa under Tudhaliya IV and proclaimed himself great king: impressions of a seal of his bearing that title were found at Hattusa, and the bronze treaty tablet was deliberately buried next to the south gate. Others think he only declared his independence or his equality with the great king, without usurping the throne; there is no agreement on what happened.

hechos/institucion-de-la-tawananna/titul.texto: The Tawananna, Queen of the Hittites

hechos/institucion-de-la-tawananna/resum.texto: Tawananna was the title of the queen of the Hittites, the king's consort for as long as she lived; at her death it passed to his daughter or to the king's new consort, not to the wife of the heir. She had religious duties as high priestess and governed when the king was on campaign; the rule caused rivalries between the new queen and the stepchildren, as the testament of Hattusili I shows.

lugares/alaca-hoyuk/resumen.texto: Site northeast of Hattusa, occupied since the Chalcolithic and famous for fourteen shaft tombs of the Early Bronze Age (c. 2850-2450 BC) with gold, silver and bronze objects. In the Hittite period it had a gate with sphinxes; its Hittite name is unknown, and it has been proposed that it was Arinna.

lugares/arslantepe/resumen.texto: Mound next to Malatya with a complex of temples and a palace from the Uruk period, violently destroyed at the end of the Late Chalcolithic, and later with Kura-Araxes pottery. In the Late Bronze Age it was the regional capital of Isuwa; Suppiluliuma I conquered it around 1350 BC.

lugares/hacinebi-tepe/resumen.texto: Site by a crossing of the Euphrates, near Birecik, with a local population of the 4th millennium BC and an enclave of the Uruk culture from c. 3700-3400 BC. It was later abandoned, except for occasional burials.

lugares/yazilikaya/resumen.texto: Rock sanctuary of Hattusa, in use since the late 16th century BC, with the most important reliefs of Hittite art. Most date from Tudhaliya IV and Suppiluliuma II, when it was restored.

lugares/sapinuwa/resumen.texto: Hittite city about 70 km east of Hattusa, a religious and administrative center, a military base and an occasional residence of kings. Some 5000 tablets and fragments from the end of the Middle Kingdom were found in Building A.

lugares/sarissa/resumen.texto: Provincial city of the Hittite highlands, founded in the 16th century BC, with the temple of the storm god, the largest Hittite temple excavated. It was sacked under Arnuwanda I, rebuilt under Tudhaliya III, and destroyed around 1200 BC.

lugares/tapikka/resumen.texto: Site occupied since the Early Bronze Age, about 100 km east of Hattusa, identified with Tapikka. Its archive of 117 tablets, mostly letters with the king, and most of them concern the front against the Kaska.

lugares/nerik/resumen.texto: Hittite holy city north of Hattusa, founded by Hattic speakers such as Narak, and seat of the cult of the storm god of Nerik. Hattusili III recovered and rebuilt it before becoming king, and it disappears from the records with the fall of the kingdom around 1200 BC. Since 2005-2009 it has been identified with Oymaağaç Höyük.

lugares/zippalanda/resumen.texto: Hattic administrative and religious center of the Old Hittite Kingdom, with a temple of the storm god, near Mount Kerkenes. The location at Uşaklı Höyük is a proposed identification.

lugares/samuha/resumen.texto: Hittite city and religious center, which was the military capital of the empire for some years during the crisis of the 14th century BC. It is proposed to locate it at Kayalıpınar, about 40 km west of Sivas, excavated since 2004.

lugares/karkemish/resumen.texto: Ancient capital of northern Syria, on the Euphrates, which was part of Mitanni and of the Hittite empire. Suppiluliuma I took it after a siege and gave it to his son Piyassili as a viceroyalty.

lugares/gozlukule/resumen.texto: Mound of Tarsus, occupied since the Neolithic, important as a port in the 2nd millennium BC at the crossroads of the coastal routes and the Cilician Gates. An impression bearing the seal of King Isputahsu of Kizzuwatna was found there.

lugares/sirkeli-hoyuk/resumen.texto: One of the largest mounds of Cilicia, beside the Ceyhan River. It was occupied from 2420 BC and had a lower town from the 17th century BC; it is said to have been abandoned in the 15th century BC and resettled after the Late Bronze collapse, although there are rock reliefs of the 13th century BC connected with Muwatalli II. It has been proposed that it is Kummanni, the capital of Kizzuwatna.

lugares/lawazantiya/resumen.texto: City of Kizzuwatna and cult center of the goddess Sauska, famous for its temple with water from seven springs. Hattusili III met Puduhepa, daughter of a priest of Sauska, there; the best candidate for the site is Tatarlı Höyük.

lugares/acemhoyuk/resumen.texto: Mound in Aksaray, a node in Anatolia's trade network in the Early Bronze Age, with an Assyrian karum and a palace of the Middle Bronze Age. It was probably Purushanda or Ullama; level III was destroyed by fire, and the site lay unoccupied until the Hellenistic or Roman period.

lugares/beycesultan/resumen.texto: Large mound in the Maeander valley, the main city of western Anatolia in the Middle Bronze Age. Its palace burned in the 17th century BC, a destruction that Mellaart attributed to Hattusili I, and the site was destroyed again around 1200 BC.

lugares/karatas-semayuk/resumen.texto: Necropolis of about 2.2 ha from the Early Bronze Age, with tombs in pithoi, and a small settlement with a mudbrick building with a palisade. Its tombs date mostly to Early Bronze II (c. 3000-2700 BC) and IIIa.

lugares/alisar-hoyuk/resumen.texto: City of central Anatolia occupied since the Neolithic, where 53 Old Assyrian tablets from a trading post were found. It has been proposed to identify it with Ankuwa, the cult center of the goddess Kataha; it suffered a widespread destruction around 1200 BC.

lugares/kaman-kalehoyuk/resumen.texto: Mound of Kırşehir about 100 km east of Ankara, with Bronze Age layers, among them Assyrian colonies and an Old Hittite kingdom level. Iron and steel dated to c. 1800 BC and glass dated to c. 1600 BC were found there.

lugares/buyukkale/resumen.texto: Rocky outcrop of Hattusa, inhabited from the end of the Early Bronze Age, which in the empire was the administrative seat of the great kings. Thousands of tablets from the archives were found there.

lugares/shengavit/resumen.texto: Fortified settlement of the Kura-Araxes culture, in Yerevan, with about 6 ha, a 4 m wide wall, metalworking and grain surpluses. It was inhabited between c. 3200 and 2500 BC and was reused until c. 2200 BC.

lugares/metsamor/resumen.texto: Fortress and city of the Ararat plain, with a stratigraphic sequence from the Early Bronze Age (Kura-Araxes culture) to modern times. Tradition said that the Urartians destroyed it in the Iron Age; today it is thought that Scythian or Cimmerian nomads did so.

lugares/lchashen/resumen.texto: Site by Lake Sevan, in Armenia, of the Late Bronze Age Lchashen-Metsamor culture, where a complete four-wheeled chariot and bronze belts were found.

lugares/kurganes-de-trialeti/resumen.texto: Group of elite mounds of the Trialeti-Vanadzor culture, in Georgia, with 46 kurgans excavated between 1936 and 1940 and six more in 1959-1962. Some held four-wheeled chariots, gold objects and a bronze cauldron similar to one from Tomb IV at Mycenae.

lugares/kurgan-de-maikop/resumen.texto: Mound about 10 m high, excavated by Nikolay Veselovsky in 1897, containing the tomb of a supposed priest-king and of two women, and figures of gold and silver bulls. It gives its name to the Maykop culture; its finds are kept at the Hermitage.

lugares/tilmen-hoyuk/resumen.texto: Mound 21 m high beside the Karasu River, on the Sakçagözü plain, occupied from the 4th millennium BC and a large city from the late 3rd millennium BC. In 2020 it was proposed to identify it with the Zalpa of the annals of Hattusili I, distinct from the Zalpuwa of the Black Sea.

lugares/zincirli/resumen.texto: Site in the Anti-Taurus, active since the Early Bronze Age and a wine trading center around 1700-1650 BC. A monumental complex of the Middle Bronze II was destroyed in the middle or late 17th century BC, perhaps by Hattusili I.

lugares/buklukale/resumen.texto: Site of about 30 ha at the narrowest crossing of the Kızılırmak, with a cyclopean wall in the lower town. It has been proposed that it was Durhumit (Turmitta) or Wahshushana, centers of Assyrian trade.

lugares/liman-tepe/resumen.texto: Early Bronze Age harbor settlement on the coast of Urla, near İzmir, with an artificial submerged harbor dating from 3300 BC and a city wall partly under the sea. It maintained links with Kastri, on Syros, and with the Cyclades.

lugares/kilise-tepe/resumen.texto: Mound beside the Göksu River, in Cilicia, occupied from the Early Bronze Age, which in the Hittite Empire controlled the route between central Anatolia and the Mediterranean ports. A Late Bronze Age level contains timber dated by dendrochronology to 1380 BC; the settlement burned at the end of the 13th century BC.

lugares/cadir-hoyuk/resumen.texto: Mound near Sorgun, about 70 km from Hattusa, with some 6000 years of occupation. It flourished between 2000 and 1100 BC and has been proposed, with doubts, as Zippalanda; recent excavations point to Uşaklı Höyük.

lugares/tyana/resumen.texto: City of Cappadocia, at present-day Kemerhisar, called Tuwanuwa in the Hittite Empire, a cult center of the storm god Tarhunza and the goddess Sahhassara. The Edict of Telipinu includes it among the territories conquered by Labarna I.

lugares/martkopi/resumen.texto: Area of eastern Georgia with rich burial mounds of the 3rd millennium BC, the early phase of the early kurgan culture of central Transcaucasia. Its kurgans are roughly contemporary with the first Trialeti mounds.

lugares/norsuntepe/resumen.texto: Mound on the upper Euphrates with 40 occupation levels, from the 5th millennium BC to c. 600 BC. In the Early Bronze Age it had a mudbrick wall on stone foundations and copper production; today it is partly covered by Lake Keban.

lugares/lidar-hoyuk/resumen.texto: Mound on the Euphrates, upstream of Samsat, with an Early Bronze Age potters' quarter and a cemetery. The Middle Bronze Age II occupation was destroyed in a large fire and reoccupied on a smaller scale in the Late Bronze Age.

lugares/degirmentepe/resumen.texto: Mound on the Euphrates, northeast of Malatya, with levels of the Chalcolithic (Ubaid period) and of the Early Bronze Age I (Karaz or Khirbet Kerak culture). The Ubaid levels have smelting of arsenical copper objects; the rescue excavations, begun in 1978, were halted in 1989 when dams flooded the site.

lugares/ikiztepe/resumen.texto: Site of four mounds and a cemetery in the Kızılırmak delta, near Bafra and the Black Sea coast. Most of what has been found dates to the Early Bronze Age, with finds possibly from the 6th millennium BC; excavation began in 1974, and some associate it with the Hittite city of Zalpuwa, although this is not certain.

lugares/konya-karahoyuk/resumen.texto: Mound 19 m high and some 33 ha (almost 100 ha including the lower town), 8 km from Konya, occupied in the Bronze Age, above all from the Middle to the Late Bronze Age. It was excavated from 1953 to 1992 under Sedat Alp and again since 2022; its bullae show contacts with Syria and the Aegean.

lugares/eflatun-pinar/resumen.texto: Spring with a monumental pool of trachyte ashlar, built in the Hittite Empire period for the cult of sacred springs, 85 km west of Konya. It is identified with the "pool of the spring of Arimatta" in the treaty of Tudhaliya IV with Kurunta of Tarhuntassa; on its face are mountain gods and a divine couple, probably the storm god and the sun goddess.

lugares/huseyindede-tepe/resumen.texto: Old Hittite site in the Sungurlu district (Çorum), surveyed in 1997. It yielded the Hüseyindede vases, with dancers, processions and figures leaping over a bull; they are of Anatolian style and not a Minoan import.

lugares/inandiktepe/resumen.texto: Mound in Çankırı province, 115 km northwest of Hattusa, with five levels, three of them from the 2nd millennium BC. In the Late Bronze Age there was a complex of some 2000 m², which the excavators variously took to be a temple and an estate, destroyed by fire.

lugares/mersin-yumuktepe/resumen.texto: Mound inside the city of Mersin, on the Cilician plain, occupied from the Neolithic to the Middle Ages. It was excavated by John Garstang (1936–1938) and, after the war, by Veli Sevin and Isabella Caneva.

lugares/hassek-hoyuk/resumen.texto: Mound on the left bank of the Euphrates, excavated before the Atatürk Dam and now underwater. It has a fortified Uruk-period acropolis, with a southern building that the excavators interpreted as a tripartite temple, and phases of the Early Bronze Age I (c. 3300–3000 BC).

lugares/kestel-y-goltepe/resumen.texto: Probable Bronze Age tin mine in the Bolkar Mountains (Taurus), with some 3 km of tunnels, and the fortified settlement of Göltepe 2 km away, which K. Aslihan Yener dated between 3290 and 1840 BC. There are crucibles with slag of high tin content; J. D. Muhly criticizes the reconstruction.

lugares/kenan-tepe/resumen.texto: Mound on the north bank of the Tigris, near Bismil, excavated between 2000 and 2008 in the area of the Ilısu Dam. It has Late Chalcolithic levels, fortifications around 3000 BC, Middle Bronze Age occupation around 1800 BC and a small Early Iron Age village.

lugares/demircihoyuk/resumen.texto: Village in northwestern Anatolia, near Eskişehir, with occupation in the Early Bronze Age I and II (c. 3000–2500 BC), an abandonment and a new occupation in the Middle Bronze Age. Some 200 clay idols and a stone casting mold were found.

lugares/kaymakci/resumen.texto: Settlement on Lake Marmara (Manisa), of at least 25 ha, with a citadel of 8.6 ha on concentric terraces, occupied from 1700 to 1200 BC and contemporary with Troy VI and VIIa. It is the main candidate for the capital of the land of the Seha River.

lugares/relieve-de-firaktin/resumen.texto: Hittite rock relief, 1.3 × 3.2 m, 50 km south of Kayseri, 13th century BC. It shows Hattusili III pouring a libation to the storm god and Puduhepa to the goddess Hepat; because the king is shown deified, it is assumed to have been made in the reign of Tudhaliya IV.

lugares/relieve-de-hanyeri/resumen.texto: Hittite rock relief of the 13th century BC beside the Gezbeli Pass, on the road from Cappadocia to Cilicia. It shows a bull standing on two mountain goddesses, named in hieroglyphs as the god Sarruma, and a border warrior, «son of a king».

lugares/relieve-de-imamkullu/resumen.texto: Hittite rock relief on a trachyte outcrop, at the northwest end of the Gezbeli Pass, in Kayseri. About 3.25 × 2 m, badly worn; the Luwian hieroglyphs name the figure on the left.

lugares/relieve-de-hemite/resumen.texto: Hittite rock relief on the north bank of the Ceyhan, at Gökçedam (Osmaniye), on the route from the Hittite heartland to Syria. It shows a warrior 1.75 m tall with spear, bow and sword; Hawkins links it with a prince Tarhuntabiya.

lugares/relieve-de-manisa/resumen.texto: Hittite rock relief 5 km east of Manisa, with a deity and two remnants of Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions. Cecil Cadoux believed it dates from the time of Suppiluliuma I or Mursili II; Bossert read «prince Kuwalanamuwa» in an inscription.

lugares/turkmen-karahoyuk/resumen.texto: Mound of some 30 ha and 35 m high on the Konya plain, inhabited from the Bronze Age to the classical period; excavated since 2017. It has been proposed as the Tarhuntassa of Muwatalli II, and in the 8th century BC it may have been the center of a kingdom of the Konya and Karaman plains.

lugares/kumtepe/resumen.texto: Earliest settlement of the Troad, with four layers: abandoned around 4500 BC and reoccupied around 3700 BC by the Kumtepe B culture, which knew copper, lead and bronze. Shortly after 3000 BC Yassıtepe and Hisarlık (Troy) are said to have been founded from there.

lugares/novosvobodnaya/resumen.texto: Megalithic tombs near the present-day village of Novosvobodnaya, in Adygea, excavated in 1898 by Nikolai Veselovsky, which give their name to an Early Bronze Age culture on the slopes of the northern Caucasus (c. 3500–3100 BC). The Klady cemetery yielded a mitochondrial genome that some relate to the Funnel Beaker culture; Rezepkin links the pottery with it.

lugares/kultepe-ii-de-najicheván/resumen.texto: Settlement in Nakhchivan, 10 km north of the city. Its oldest layer, 7 to 10 m deep, is Early Bronze Age and of the Kura-Araxes culture (radiocarbon dates of 3500–2400 BC); the 2nd-millennium layer, with walls and buildings, is when it reached its greatest extent.

lugares/uzerliktapa/resumen.texto: Middle Bronze Age settlement near Agdam, in Karabakh, excavated since 1954, with a cultural layer some 3.5 m deep from the late 2nd millennium BC. It yielded grape seeds, bronze objects and the remains of a fire.

lugares/mingachevir/resumen.texto: Complex of four settlements and four cemeteries on both banks of the Kura, in Azerbaijan, from the Early Bronze Age (3rd millennium BC) to the late Middle Ages. Its oldest layer is of the Kura-Araxes culture; the second is of the Khojaly-Gadabay culture (late 2nd and early 1st millennium BC).

lugares/ergeta/resumen.texto: Group of more than twenty mounds in Colchis, at Zugdidi (Georgia), continuously occupied from the early 2nd millennium BC. It has Bronze Age wooden houses, a socketed bronze axe and casting molds; it has been excavated since 1978.

lugares/golpinar-dam/resumen.texto: Hittite dam of the 2nd millennium BC, 1.5 km southeast of Alaca Höyük, with a rectangular pool of about 110 by 100 m and a Luwian hieroglyphic inscription dedicated to the goddess Hepat. It is attributed to Tudhaliya IV, who according to a cuneiform document had dams built around 1240 BC after a drought.

lugares/karashamb/resumen.texto: Village in Kotayk province, Armenia, with a large excavation of a Bronze Age cemetery of burial mounds. In the richest one, a «royal» tomb, a silver cup appeared, which is now one of the treasures of the National Museum.

lugares/dolmenes-del-caucaso-norte/nombr.texto: Dolmens of the northern Caucasus (area; no precise site)

lugares/dolmenes-del-caucaso-norte/resum.texto: Some 3000 dolmens and stone labyrinths of the western Caucasus, from the late 4th to the early 2nd millennium BC, across some 12,000 km² in Russia and Abkhazia. They are rectangular chambers of slabs or cut into the rock, with holes in the facade; their origin is unknown.

lugares/karabel/resumen.texto: Hittite-Luwian rock relief at the Karabel Pass, about 20 km from Smyrna, with a warrior with bow and spear. A Luwian hieroglyphic inscription identifies him with Tarkasnawa, king of Mira in the 13th century BC, and proves that Mira was south of the land of the Seha River.
